Of government the properties to unfold / Would seem in me t' affect speech and discourse, / Since I am put to know that your own science / Exceeds, in that, the lists of all advice / My strength can give you. Then no more remains / But that, to your sufficiency, as your worth is able, / And let them work. The nature of our people, / Our city's institutions, and the terms / For common justice, you're as pregnant in / As art and practice hath enriched any / That we remember. There is our commission, / From which we would not have you warp.—Call hither, / I say, bid come before us, Angelo.

To lecture you on the principles of government would only make me look as if I loved the sound of my own voice, since I know your own knowledge of it goes beyond any advice I could give. So all that is left is to add authority to your ability, and let the two work together. You know our people's character, our city's institutions and the workings of public justice as well as anyone I can remember, in both theory and practice. Here is your commission; do not stray from it. (To an Attendant) Go and tell Angelo to come here.

What figure of us think you he will bear? / For you must know we have with special soul / Elected him our absence to supply; / Lent him our terror, drest him with our love, / And given his deputation all the organs / Of our own power. What think you of it?

How do you think he will carry my role? You must know that I have deliberately chosen him to fill my place while I am away. I have lent him my power to punish, dressed him in my love, and given his deputyship every instrument of my own authority. What do you think of it?
If any in Vienna be of worth / To undergo such ample grace and honour, / It is Lord Angelo.
If anyone in Vienna is worthy of such great honour and favour, it is Lord Angelo.
Always obedient to your Grace's will, / I come to know your pleasure.
Always ready to obey your Grace, I have come to hear what you want.

Angelo, / There is a kind of character in thy life / That to th' observer doth thy history / Fully unfold. Thyself and thy belongings / Are not thine own so proper as to waste / Thyself upon thy virtues, they on thee. / Heaven doth with us as we with torches do, / Not light them for themselves; for if our virtues / Did not go forth of us, 'twere all alike / As if we had them not. Spirits are not finely touched / But to fine issues; nor nature never lends / The smallest scruple of her excellence / But, like a thrifty goddess, she determines / Herself the glory of a creditor, / Both thanks and use. But I do bend my speech / To one that can my part in him advertise. / Hold, therefore, Angelo. / In our remove be thou at full ourself. / Mortality and mercy in Vienna / Live in thy tongue and heart. Old Escalus, / Though first in question, is thy secondary. / Take thy commission.

Angelo, there is something in the way you live that tells anyone watching your whole story. You and your gifts do not belong to you so completely that you may spend yourself on your virtues, or they on you. Heaven treats us the way we treat torches: we do not light them for their own sake. If our virtues did not shine out from us, we might as well not have them. Fine spirits are given for fine purposes, and nature never lends even the smallest piece of her excellence without claiming, like a careful lender, both thanks and interest. But I am speaking to a man who could teach me my own part. So take this, Angelo. While I am away, be me in full. Death and mercy in Vienna live in your tongue and your heart. Old Escalus, though he was asked first, is your second in command. Take your commission.
Now, good my lord, / Let there be some more test made of my metal, / Before so noble and so great a figure / Be stamped upon it.
But my lord, test my metal a little more before such a great and noble stamp is pressed onto it.

No more evasion. / We have with a leavened and prepared choice / Proceeded to you; therefore take your honours. / Our haste from hence is of so quick condition / That it prefers itself, and leaves unquestioned / Matters of needful value. We shall write to you, / As time and our concernings shall importune, / How it goes with us; and do look to know / What doth befall you here. So, fare you well. / To th' hopeful execution do I leave you / Of your commissions.

No more excuses. I chose you after careful thought, so accept the honour. I have to leave so quickly that more important matters must wait. I will write to you when time and my affairs allow, telling you how things go with me, and I expect to hear what happens here. So, goodbye. I leave you to carry out your commissions, and I hope you do it well.
Yet give leave, my lord, / That we may bring you something on the way.
At least let us go with you part of the way, my lord.

My haste may not admit it; / Nor need you, on mine honour, have to do / With any scruple. Your scope is as mine own, / So to enforce or qualify the laws / As to your soul seems good. Give me your hand; / I'll privily away. I love the people, / But do not like to stage me to their eyes. / Though it do well, I do not relish well / Their loud applause and Aves vehement; / Nor do I think the man of safe discretion / That does affect it. Once more, fare you well.

I am in too much of a hurry for that, and on my honour you need have no doubts. Your power is as great as mine, to enforce the laws strictly or to soften them as your conscience thinks right. Give me your hand. I will slip away quietly. I love the people, but I do not like to parade myself in front of them. It may be well meant, but I take no pleasure in their loud cheering and shouting; and I do not think a man with any judgment seeks it. Once again, goodbye.
The heavens give safety to your purposes!
May heaven keep you safe in what you do!
Lead forth and bring you back in happiness.
May it lead you out and bring you back happily.
I thank you. Fare you well.

I shall desire you, sir, to give me leave / To have free speech with you; and it concerns me / To look into the bottom of my place. / A power I have, but of what strength and nature / I am not yet instructed.
Sir, I would like to talk frankly with you. I need to understand exactly what my position is. I have been given power, but nobody has told me how far it reaches or what kind it is.
'Tis so with me. Let us withdraw together, / And we may soon our satisfaction have / Touching that point.
It is the same with me. Let us go somewhere private and soon settle the question.
If the Duke, with the other dukes, come not to composition with the / King of Hungary, why then all the dukes fall upon the King.
If the Duke and the other dukes do not come to terms with the King of Hungary, then all the dukes will attack the King.
Heaven grant us its peace, but not the King of Hungary's!
God give us peace, but not the King of Hungary's peace!
Thou conclud'st like the sanctimonious pirate that went to sea with the / ten commandments, but scraped one out of the table.
You end that like the holy-looking pirate who went to sea with the Ten Commandments but scratched one off the tablet.
Yes, that's the one he rubbed out.

Why, 'twas a commandment to command the captain and all the rest from / their functions! They put forth to steal. There's not a soldier of us / all that, in the thanksgiving before meat, do relish the petition well / that prays for peace.

Of course: that commandment would have put the captain and all his crew out of work. They set out to steal. There's not one soldier among us who enjoys the bit of grace before dinner that prays for peace.
I never heard any soldier dislike it.
I never heard a soldier who disliked it.
I believe thee; for I think thou never wast where grace was said.
I believe you, because I don't think you've ever been anywhere grace was said.
No? A dozen times at least.
No? At least a dozen times.
In any proportion or in any language.
In any form and in any language.
I think, or in any religion.
And in any religion, I suppose.
Ay, why not? Grace is grace, despite of all controversy; as, for / example, thou thyself art a wicked villain, despite of all grace.
Yes, why not? Grace is grace whatever the arguments, just as you, for example, are a wicked villain whatever grace you have.
Well, there went but a pair of shears between us.
Well, we're cut from the same cloth.
I grant, as there may between the lists and the velvet. Thou art the / list.
Agreed, just as the plain edging and the velvet are cut from the same piece. You're the edging.

And thou the velvet. Thou art good velvet; thou'rt a three-piled piece, / I warrant thee. I had as lief be a list of an English kersey as be / piled, as thou art piled, for a French velvet. Do I speak feelingly / now?

And you're the velvet. Good velvet too, thick triple pile, I'm sure. I'd rather be the plain edge of an English woollen than be bald like you, rubbed bare by French velvet. Have I touched a sore spot?
I think thou dost, and indeed, with most painful feeling of thy speech. / I will, out of thine own confession, learn to begin thy health; but, / whilst I live, forget to drink after thee.
I think you have, and you speak like a man in real pain. Since you've confessed it, I'll drink your health first, but as long as I live I'll never drink from the same cup after you.
I think I have done myself wrong, have I not?
I think I've done myself harm there, haven't I?
Yes, that thou hast, whether thou art tainted or free.
Yes, you have, whether you're infected or not.
Behold, behold, where Madam Mitigation comes! I have purchased as many / diseases under her roof as come to—
Look, look, here comes Madam Mitigation! I've caught as many diseases under her roof as would add up to...
To three thousand dolours a year.
To three thousand dollars' worth of pain a year.
Thou art always figuring diseases in me, but thou art full of error; I / am sound.
You're always imagining diseases in me, but you're wrong: I'm sound.
Nay, not, as one would say, healthy, but so sound as things that are / hollow. Thy bones are hollow. Impiety has made a feast of thee.
No, not sound as in healthy, but sound like something hollow when you knock it. Your bones are hollow. Sin has feasted on you.
How now, which of your hips has the most profound sciatica?
Well now, which of your hips has the worst sciatica?
Well, well! There's one yonder arrested and carried to prison was worth / five thousand of you all.
Well, well. There's a man down there who has been arrested and taken to prison who was worth five thousand of you all.
Marry, sir, that's Claudio, Signior Claudio.
Why, sir, it's Claudio, Signior Claudio.
Claudio in prison? It can't be true.
Nay, but I know 'tis so. I saw him arrested, saw him carried away; and, / which is more, within these three days his head to be chopped off.
No, I know it's true. I saw him arrested and taken away. What's more, in three days' time his head is to be chopped off.
But, after all this fooling, I would not have it so. Art thou sure of / this?
All joking aside, I would hate that to happen. Are you sure?
I am too sure of it. And it is for getting Madam Julietta with child.
I'm only too sure. And it's for getting Madam Julietta pregnant.
Believe me, this may be. He promised to meet me two hours since, and he / was ever precise in promise-keeping.
Believe me, this could be true. He promised to meet me two hours ago, and he always keeps his appointments exactly.
Besides, you know, it draws something near to the speech we had to such / a purpose.
Besides, you know, it fits with what we were saying earlier.
But most of all agreeing with the proclamation.
And most of all it fits the new proclamation.
Away! Let's go learn the truth of it.
Come on! Let's go and find out the truth.
Thus, what with the war, what with the sweat, what with the gallows, / and what with poverty, I am custom-shrunk.
So what with the war, the sweating sickness, the gallows and poverty, I'm losing all my customers.
How now? What's the news with you?
Yonder man is carried to prison.
That man over there is being taken to prison.
Groping for trouts in a peculiar river.
Tickling for trout in a private river.
What? Is there a maid with child by him?
What? Has he made a girl pregnant?
No, but there's a woman with maid by him. You have not heard of the / proclamation, have you?
No, but he's made a woman out of a girl. Haven't you heard about the proclamation?
All houses in the suburbs of Vienna must be plucked down.
All the brothels in the suburbs of Vienna are to be torn down.
And what shall become of those in the city?
And what will happen to the ones in the city?
They shall stand for seed. They had gone down too, but that a wise / burgher put in for them.
They'll be left standing, for breeding. They'd have come down too, but a wise citizen put in a word for them.
But shall all our houses of resort in the suburbs be pulled down?
But are all our houses of business in the suburbs to be pulled down?
Why, here's a change indeed in the commonwealth! What shall become of / me?
Well, here's a change in the state of things! What will become of me?

Come, fear not you. Good counsellors lack no clients. Though you change / your place, you need not change your trade. I'll be your tapster still. / Courage, there will be pity taken on you. You that have worn your eyes / almost out in the service, you will be considered.

Come on, don't worry. A good lawyer never lacks clients. You may change your address, but you needn't change your trade. I'll still be your barman. Cheer up, people will take pity on you. You've almost worn out your eyes in the service; you'll be looked after.
What's to do here, Thomas Tapster? Let's withdraw.
What's going on here, Thomas the barman? Let's get out of the way.
Here comes Signior Claudio, led by the Provost to prison. And there's / Madam Juliet.
Here comes Signior Claudio, being taken to prison by the Provost. And there's Madam Juliet.
Fellow, why dost thou show me thus to the world? / Bear me to prison, where I am committed.
Why do you parade me in front of everyone like this, fellow? Take me to the prison I've been sent to.
I do it not in evil disposition, / But from Lord Angelo by special charge.
I don't do it out of spite, but on Lord Angelo's particular orders.
Thus can the demi-god Authority / Make us pay down for our offence by weight. / The words of heaven; on whom it will, it will; / On whom it will not, so; yet still 'tis just.
So the half-god Authority can make us pay for our crimes in full measure. It is like the word of heaven: it strikes whoever it chooses and spares whoever it chooses, and still it is always just.
Why, how now, Claudio? Whence comes this restraint?
Claudio, what's this? Why are you under arrest?

From too much liberty, my Lucio, liberty. / As surfeit is the father of much fast, / So every scope by the immoderate use / Turns to restraint. Our natures do pursue, / Like rats that ravin down their proper bane, / A thirsty evil; and when we drink, we die.

From too much freedom, my Lucio, freedom. Just as overeating leads to fasting, so every liberty, used without limit, turns into restraint. Our natures chase after a thirst for evil the way rats greedily swallow the poison meant for them; and when we drink, we die.

If I could speak so wisely under an arrest, I would send for certain of / my creditors; and yet, to say the truth, I had as lief have the foppery / of freedom as the morality of imprisonment. What's thy offence, / Claudio?

If I could talk that wisely under arrest, I would send for some of my creditors. But to tell the truth, I'd rather have the foolishness of freedom than the wisdom of prison. What have you done, Claudio?
What but to speak of would offend again.
Something I would offend again just by talking about it.
Come along, sir; you have to go.
One word, good friend.—Lucio, a word with you.
Just one word, good friend. Lucio, a word with you.
A hundred, if they'll do you any good. Is lechery so looked after?
A hundred, if they'll help you. Is lechery so closely watched now?

Thus stands it with me: upon a true contract / I got possession of Julietta's bed. / You know the lady; she is fast my wife, / Save that we do the denunciation lack / Of outward order. This we came not to / Only for propagation of a dower / Remaining in the coffer of her friends, / From whom we thought it meet to hide our love / Till time had made them for us. But it chances / The stealth of our most mutual entertainment / With character too gross is writ on Juliet.

This is my situation. Under a binding contract of marriage, I slept with Julietta. You know the lady. She is truly my wife, except that we have not made the public announcement in church. We held back from that only so that her dowry, which is still held by her relatives, would come to us; we thought it best to hide our love from them until time had won them over to us. But as it happens, the secret of our love for each other is now written too plainly on Juliet's body.

Unhappily, even so. / And the new deputy now for the Duke— / Whether it be the fault and glimpse of newness, / Or whether that the body public be / A horse whereon the governor doth ride, / Who, newly in the seat, that it may know / He can command, lets it straight feel the spur; / Whether the tyranny be in his place, / Or in his eminence that fills it up, / I stagger in—but this new governor / Awakes me all the enrolled penalties / Which have, like unscoured armour, hung by th' wall / So long that nineteen zodiacs have gone round, / And none of them been worn; and for a name / Now puts the drowsy and neglected act / Freshly on me. 'Tis surely for a name.

Unfortunately, yes. And the Duke's new deputy, whether it is the mistake and glare of being new, or whether he thinks the people are a horse for the ruler to ride, and that a new rider must use the spur at once to show he is in charge, whether the tyranny lies in the office or in the man who holds it, I can't tell; but this new governor has woken up every penalty in the statute book that has hung unused on the wall like rusty armour for nineteen years. To make a name for himself he has dug out this sleepy, forgotten law and applied it fresh to me. It must be to make a name.
I warrant it is. And thy head stands so tickle on thy shoulders that a / milkmaid, if she be in love, may sigh it off. Send after the Duke, and / appeal to him.
I'm sure it is. And your head sits so loosely on your shoulders that a lovesick milkmaid could sigh it off. Send a message to the Duke and appeal to him.

I have done so, but he's not to be found. / I prithee, Lucio, do me this kind service: / This day my sister should the cloister enter, / And there receive her approbation. / Acquaint her with the danger of my state; / Implore her, in my voice, that she make friends / To the strict deputy; bid herself assay him. / I have great hope in that. For in her youth / There is a prone and speechless dialect / Such as moves men; beside, she hath prosperous art / When she will play with reason and discourse, / And well she can persuade.

I have, but he can't be found. Please, Lucio, do me this favour. Today my sister is due to enter the convent and begin her trial as a novice. Tell her what danger I'm in. Beg her, from me, to make friends with the strict deputy and try to win him over herself. I have great hopes of that. In her youth there is a silent, willing language that moves men; and besides, she has a real gift when she uses argument and reason, and she can be very persuasive.

I pray she may, as well for the encouragement of the like, which else / would stand under grievous imposition, as for the enjoying of thy life, / who I would be sorry should be thus foolishly lost at a game of / tick-tack. I'll to her.

I hope she can, both to encourage others like you, who would otherwise be in serious danger, and so you can keep your life. I would hate to see it thrown away so stupidly over a game of tick-tack. I'll go to her.
I thank you, good friend Lucio.

No, holy father, throw away that thought; / Believe not that the dribbling dart of love / Can pierce a complete bosom. Why I desire thee / To give me secret harbour hath a purpose / More grave and wrinkled than the aims and ends / Of burning youth.

No, holy father, put that idea out of your head. Don't think love's feeble little arrow can pierce a heart as armoured as mine. My reason for asking you to hide me secretly is far more serious and mature than the aims of hot-blooded young men.
May your Grace speak of it?
May your Grace tell me what it is?

My holy sir, none better knows than you / How I have ever loved the life removed, / And held in idle price to haunt assemblies / Where youth, and cost, a witless bravery keeps. / I have delivered to Lord Angelo, / A man of stricture and firm abstinence, / My absolute power and place here in Vienna, / And he supposes me travelled to Poland; / For so I have strewed it in the common ear, / And so it is received. Now, pious sir, / You will demand of me why I do this?

My holy sir, nobody knows better than you how I have always loved a quiet, private life, and thought little of going where young people gather and spend money on empty show. I have handed my complete power and position here in Vienna to Lord Angelo, a man of strict discipline and firm self-denial, and he thinks I have gone to Poland. That is the story I have spread among the people, and they believe it. Now, good sir, you will want to know why I am doing this.

We have strict statutes and most biting laws, / The needful bits and curbs to headstrong weeds, / Which for this fourteen years we have let slip, / Even like an o'ergrown lion in a cave / That goes not out to prey. Now, as fond fathers, / Having bound up the threat'ning twigs of birch, / Only to stick it in their children's sight / For terror, not to use, in time the rod / Becomes more mocked than feared: so our decrees, / Dead to infliction, to themselves are dead, / And liberty plucks justice by the nose, / The baby beats the nurse, and quite athwart / Goes all decorum.

We have strict statutes and harsh laws, the necessary bits and bridles for wild horses, which for fourteen years we have let lapse, like an overgrown lion in a cave that never goes out to hunt. Foolish fathers tie up a threatening bundle of birch twigs and only display it to frighten their children, never to use it, so that in time the rod is mocked instead of feared. In the same way our laws, never enforced, are as good as dead. Freedom pulls justice by the nose, the baby hits the nurse, and all good order is turned upside down.
It rested in your Grace / To unloose this tied-up justice when you pleased; / And it in you more dreadful would have seemed / Than in Lord Angelo.
Your Grace had the power to set this tied-up justice loose whenever you wanted, and it would have seemed more frightening coming from you than from Lord Angelo.

I do fear, too dreadful. / Sith 'twas my fault to give the people scope, / 'Twould be my tyranny to strike and gall them / For what I bid them do; for we bid this be done / When evil deeds have their permissive pass / And not the punishment. Therefore, indeed, my father, / I have on Angelo imposed the office; / Who may in th' ambush of my name strike home, / And yet my nature never in the fight / To do in slander. And to behold his sway, / I will, as 'twere a brother of your order, / Visit both prince and people. Therefore, I prithee, / Supply me with the habit, and instruct me / How I may formally in person bear / Like a true friar. Moe reasons for this action / At our more leisure shall I render you; / Only, this one: Lord Angelo is precise; / Stands at a guard with envy; scarce confesses / That his blood flows or that his appetite / Is more to bread than stone. Hence shall we see, / If power change purpose, what our seemers be.

Too frightening, I fear. Since it was my fault that the people were given such freedom, it would be tyranny for me to punish and hurt them for what I let them do; for when we let wrongdoing pass unpunished, we as good as order it. That, father, is why I have given the office to Angelo. He can strike hard while hiding behind my name, and my own reputation will not be damaged in the fight. And to watch how he rules, I will visit both prince and people as if I were a friar of your order. So please, give me the habit and teach me how to carry myself like a real friar. I will give you more reasons for this when we have more time. Just this one: Lord Angelo is strict. He stands on guard against malice and will hardly admit that blood runs in his veins, or that he would rather eat bread than stone. So we shall see, if power changes a man's aims, what these people who only seem good are really like.
And have you nuns no farther privileges?
Do you nuns have no other privileges?
Yes, truly; I speak not as desiring more, / But rather wishing a more strict restraint / Upon the sisterhood, the votarists of Saint Clare.
Yes, really. I'm not asking for more; I'd rather wish for stricter rules for the sisterhood, the devoted servants of Saint Clare.
[Within] Ho! Peace be in this place!
(Calling from outside) Hello! Peace be in this place!

It is a man's voice. Gentle Isabella, / Turn you the key, and know his business of him; / You may, I may not; you are yet unsworn. / When you have vowed, you must not speak with men / But in the presence of the prioress; / Then, if you speak, you must not show your face; / Or if you show your face, you must not speak. / He calls again. I pray you answer him.

It's a man's voice. Gentle Isabella, unlock the door and find out what he wants. You may; I may not, because you have not taken your vows yet. Once you have, you may not talk to men except in the presence of the prioress, and then if you speak you must not show your face, or if you show your face you must not speak. He's calling again. Please answer him.
Peace and prosperity! Who is't that calls?
Peace and prosperity! Who is calling?

Hail, virgin, if you be, as those cheek-roses / Proclaim you are no less. Can you so stead me / As bring me to the sight of Isabella, / A novice of this place, and the fair sister / To her unhappy brother Claudio?
Hello, maiden, if that is what you are, as those rosy cheeks say you are. Can you help me to see Isabella, a novice here and the beautiful sister of her unhappy brother Claudio?
Why "her unhappy brother"? let me ask, / The rather for I now must make you know / I am that Isabella, and his sister.
Why "her unhappy brother", may I ask? I ask because I must tell you that I am that Isabella, and his sister.
Gentle and fair, your brother kindly greets you. / Not to be weary with you, he's in prison.
Gentle and beautiful lady, your brother sends you his love. To keep it short, he is in prison.
For that which, if myself might be his judge, / He should receive his punishment in thanks: / He hath got his friend with child.
For something that, if I were his judge, would earn him thanks instead of punishment. He has made his girlfriend pregnant.
Sir, make me not your story.
Sir, don't make fun of me.

'Tis true. / I would not, though 'tis my familiar sin / With maids to seem the lapwing, and to jest, / Tongue far from heart, play with all virgins so. / I hold you as a thing enskied and sainted / By your renouncement an immortal spirit, / And to be talked with in sincerity, / As with a saint.

It's true. It is my usual fault to play the lapwing with girls, teasing them with words that are far from my heart, but I would never treat all maidens like that. I think of you as someone set in heaven and made a saint, an immortal spirit because you have given up the world, and to be spoken to honestly, as one would speak to a saint.
You do blaspheme the good in mocking me.
You insult goodness by mocking me.

Do not believe it. Fewness and truth, 'tis thus: / Your brother and his lover have embraced; / As those that feed grow full, as blossoming time / That from the seedness the bare fallow brings / To teeming foison, even so her plenteous womb / Expresseth his full tilth and husbandry.

Don't think that. In short, and truly: your brother and his lover have slept together. Just as people who eat grow full, and as springtime turns the bare ploughed field into a rich harvest, so her fruitful womb shows how well he has tilled and farmed.
Someone with child by him? My cousin Juliet?
Someone is pregnant by him? My cousin Juliet?
Adoptedly, as school-maids change their names / By vain though apt affection.
Only by choice, the way schoolgirls give each other new names out of silly but natural affection.

This is the point. / The Duke is very strangely gone from hence; / Bore many gentlemen, myself being one, / In hand, and hope of action; but we do learn, / By those that know the very nerves of state, / His givings-out were of an infinite distance / From his true-meant design. Upon his place, / And with full line of his authority, / Governs Lord Angelo; a man whose blood / Is very snow-broth; one who never feels / The wanton stings and motions of the sense; / But doth rebate and blunt his natural edge / With profits of the mind, study and fast. / He, to give fear to use and liberty, / Which have for long run by the hideous law / As mice by lions, hath picked out an act, / Under whose heavy sense your brother's life / Falls into forfeit. He arrests him on it, / And follows close the rigour of the statute / To make him an example. All hope is gone, / Unless you have the grace by your fair prayer / To soften Angelo. And that's my pith of business / 'Twixt you and your poor brother.

That's the point. The Duke has left here very mysteriously. He led many gentlemen, me among them, to expect military action, but we hear from people who know the inner workings of the state that what he said was miles away from what he really intended. Lord Angelo now rules in his place, with all his authority. He is a man whose blood is melted snow, who never feels the playful stings and impulses of the senses, but dulls and blunts his natural desires with improving the mind, study and fasting. To frighten people out of the habit of freedom, which has long run past the terrible law like mice past lions, he has picked out a statute under whose harsh terms your brother's life is forfeit. He has arrested him under it and is following the strict letter of the law to make an example of him. There is no hope left, unless you can soften Angelo with your sweet pleading. And that is the heart of my business between you and your poor brother.
Doth he so / Seek his life?
Does he really want his life?
Has censured him already; / And, as I hear, the Provost hath a warrant / For's execution.
He has sentenced him already, and I hear the Provost has a warrant for his execution.
Alas, what poor ability's in me / To do him good?
Oh, what little power I have to help him!
My power? I'm afraid I doubt it.

Our doubts are traitors, / And make us lose the good we oft might win / By fearing to attempt. Go to Lord Angelo, / And let him learn to know, when maidens sue, / Men give like gods; but when they weep and kneel, / All their petitions are as freely theirs / As they themselves would owe them.

Our doubts are traitors. They make us lose the good we might often win by making us afraid to try. Go to Lord Angelo and let him learn that when young women plead, men give like gods; and when they weep and kneel, they get whatever they ask for as if it were already theirs.
I'll see what I can do.
I'll see what I can do.
I will about it straight; / No longer staying but to give the Mother / Notice of my affair. I humbly thank you. / Commend me to my brother. Soon at night / I'll send him certain word of my success.
I'll go at once, stopping only to tell the Mother Superior what I'm doing. Thank you very much. Give my love to my brother. Early this evening I'll send him word of how I get on.
I take my leave of you.
We must not make a scarecrow of the law, / Setting it up to fear the birds of prey, / And let it keep one shape till custom make it / Their perch, and not their terror.
We must not turn the law into a scarecrow, put up to frighten the birds of prey, and leave it standing the same until they get used to it and use it as a perch instead of fearing it.

Ay, but yet / Let us be keen, and rather cut a little / Than fall and bruise to death. Alas, this gentleman, / Whom I would save, had a most noble father. / Let but your honour know, / Whom I believe to be most strait in virtue, / That, in the working of your own affections, / Had time cohered with place, or place with wishing, / Or that the resolute acting of your blood / Could have attained th' effect of your own purpose, / Whether you had not sometime in your life / Erred in this point which now you censure him, / And pulled the law upon you.

Yes, but still, let us be sharp and cut a little rather than knock a man down and crush him to death. This gentleman, whom I would like to save, had a very noble father. Just think, your honour, though I believe you are perfectly upright: if in the heat of your own feelings time had fitted with place, or place with desire, or if your passion had been able to get what it wanted, consider whether you might not once in your life have done the very thing you are condemning him for, and brought the law down on yourself.

'Tis one thing to be tempted, Escalus, / Another thing to fall. I not deny / The jury passing on the prisoner's life / May in the sworn twelve have a thief or two / Guiltier than him they try. What's open made to justice, / That justice seizes. What knows the laws / That thieves do pass on thieves? 'Tis very pregnant, / The jewel that we find, we stoop and take 't, / Because we see it; but what we do not see, / We tread upon, and never think of it. / You may not so extenuate his offence / For I have had such faults; but rather tell me, / When I that censure him do so offend, / Let mine own judgement pattern out my death, / And nothing come in partial. Sir, he must die.

Being tempted is one thing, Escalus; falling is another. I do not deny that a jury of twelve men deciding a prisoner's life may include a thief or two who are guiltier than the man they are trying. Justice seizes what is brought before it. What does the law know about thieves sentencing thieves? It is obvious: if we see a jewel, we bend down and pick it up because we see it; but what we don't see, we tread on without a thought. You cannot excuse his crime because I have had such faults. Instead, tell me this: if I who sentence him ever commit the same offence, let my own judgment set the pattern for my death, and let nothing soften it. Sir, he must die.
Be it as your wisdom will.
Here, if it like your honour.
Here, if it please your honour.
See that Claudio / Be executed by nine tomorrow morning. / Bring him his confessor, let him be prepared, / For that's the utmost of his pilgrimage.
Make sure Claudio is executed by nine o'clock tomorrow morning. Bring him his confessor and let him be prepared, because that is the end of his journey.
Well, heaven forgive him; and forgive us all. / Some rise by sin, and some by virtue fall. / Some run from brakes of vice, and answer none, / And some condemned for a fault alone.

Well, heaven forgive him, and forgive us all. Some rise through sin, and some fall through virtue. Some escape from thickets of vice and never answer for it, and some are condemned for a single fault.
Come, bring them away. If these be good people in a commonweal that do / nothing but use their abuses in common houses, I know no law. Bring / them away.
Come on, bring them along. If these are good citizens of the commonwealth, who do nothing but carry on their abuses in common brothels, then I know nothing about the law. Bring them along.
How now, sir, what's your name? And what's the matter?
Well, sir, what's your name? And what's the problem?
If it please your honour, I am the poor Duke's constable, and my name / is Elbow. I do lean upon justice, sir, and do bring in here before your / good honour two notorious benefactors.

If it please your honour, I am the poor Duke's constable, and my name is Elbow. I lean on justice, sir, and I bring here before your honour two notorious benefactors (he means malefactors, criminals).
Benefactors? Well, what benefactors are they? Are they not malefactors?
Benefactors? Well, what benefactors are they? Don't you mean malefactors?
If it please your honour, I know not well what they are, but precise / villains they are, that I am sure of, and void of all profanation in / the world that good Christians ought to have.
If it please your honour, I don't really know what they are, but they're downright villains, I'm sure of that, and empty of all the profanity (he means piety) that good Christians ought to have.
This comes off well. Here's a wise officer.
This is going well. What a wise officer.
Go to. What quality are they of? Elbow is your name? Why dost thou not / speak, Elbow?
Come on. What sort of people are they? Your name is Elbow? Why don't you speak, Elbow?
He cannot, sir. He's out at elbow.
He can't, sir. He's out at elbow (worn out, at a loss).

He, sir? A tapster, sir; parcel bawd; one that serves a bad woman; / whose house, sir, was, as they say, plucked down in the suburbs; and / now she professes a hot-house, which, I think is a very ill house too.

Him, sir? A barman, sir, and part pimp. He works for a bad woman whose house, sir, was, as they say, pulled down in the suburbs; and now she claims to run a bath-house, which I think is a very bad house too.
My wife, sir, whom I detest before heaven and your honour—
My wife, sir, whom I detest (he means protest) before heaven and your honour...
Ay, sir, whom I thank heaven is an honest woman—
Yes, sir, and I thank heaven she is an honest woman...
So you detest her for that?
I say, sir, I will detest myself also, as well as she, that this house, / if it be not a bawd's house, it is pity of her life, for it is a / naughty house.
I say, sir, I will detest myself as well as her that this house, if it isn't a brothel, it's a shame she's alive, because it's a wicked house.
How dost thou know that, constable?
How do you know that, constable?
Marry, sir, by my wife, who, if she had been a woman cardinally given, / might have been accused in fornication, adultery, and all uncleanliness / there.
Why, sir, through my wife, who, if she had been a woman cardinally (he means carnally) inclined, might have been accused of fornication, adultery and every kind of filth there.
Ay, sir, by Mistress Overdone's means; but as she spit in his face, so / she defied him.
Yes, sir, through Mistress Overdone's doing. But since she spat in his face, she defied him.
Sir, if it please your honour, this is not so.
Sir, if it please your honour, that's not true.
Prove it before these varlets here, thou honourable man, prove it.
Prove it in front of these villains here, you honourable man, prove it.
[To Angelo] Do you hear how he misplaces?
(To Angelo) Do you hear how he gets his words in the wrong place?

Sir, she came in great with child; and longing, saving your honour's / reverence, for stewed prunes; sir, we had but two in the house, which / at that very distant time stood, as it were, in a fruit dish, a dish of / some threepence; your honours have seen such dishes; they are not china / dishes, but very good dishes—

Sir, she came in heavily pregnant, and longing, begging your honour's pardon, for stewed prunes. Sir, we had only two in the house, which at that very distant time stood, as it were, in a fruit dish, a dish worth about threepence. Your honours have seen such dishes; they aren't china dishes, but very good dishes...
Go to, go to. No matter for the dish, sir.
Come on, come on. Never mind the dish, sir.

No, indeed, sir, not of a pin; you are therein in the right. But to the / point. As I say, this Mistress Elbow, being, as I say, with child, and / being great-bellied, and longing, as I said, for prunes; and having but / two in the dish, as I said, Master Froth here, this very man, having / eaten the rest, as I said, and, as I say, paying for them very / honestly; for, as you know, Master Froth, I could not give you / threepence again—

No, indeed, sir, it doesn't matter a pin; you're quite right there. But to the point. As I say, this Mistress Elbow being, as I say, pregnant, and big-bellied, and longing, as I said, for prunes, and there being only two in the dish, as I said, Master Froth here, this very man, having eaten the rest, as I said, and, as I say, paying for them very honestly, for, as you know, Master Froth, I couldn't give you threepence change...
Very well. You being then, if you be remembered, cracking the stones of / the foresaid prunes—
Very well. You were then, if you remember, cracking the stones of the said prunes...
Why, very well. I telling you then, if you be remembered, that such a / one and such a one were past cure of the thing you wot of, unless they / kept very good diet, as I told you—
Why, very well. I was telling you then, if you remember, that so-and-so and so-and-so were past curing of the thing you know about, unless they kept to a very careful diet, as I told you...
Come, you are a tedious fool. To the purpose. What was done to Elbow's / wife that he hath cause to complain of? Come me to what was done to / her.
Come on, you're a tiresome fool. Get to the point. What was done to Elbow's wife that he has reason to complain about? Get me to what was done to her.
Sir, your honour cannot come to that yet.
Sir, your honour can't come to that yet.
No, sir, nor I mean it not.
No, sir, and I don't intend to.

Sir, but you shall come to it, by your honour's leave. And I beseech / you, look into Master Froth here, sir, a man of fourscore pound a year; / whose father died at Hallowmas—was't not at Hallowmas, Master Froth?

But you shall come to it, sir, with your honour's permission. And I beg you, take a look at Master Froth here, sir, a man with eighty pounds a year, whose father died at Hallowmas. Wasn't it at Hallowmas, Master Froth?
Why, very well. I hope here be truths. He, sir, sitting, as I say, in a / lower chair, sir—'twas in the Bunch of Grapes, where, indeed, you have / a delight to sit, have you not?
Why, very well. I hope these are truths. He, sir, sitting, as I say, in a low chair, sir, it was in the Bunch of Grapes room, where you do like to sit, don't you?
I have so, because it is an open room, and good for winter.
I do, because it's an open room and good in winter.
Why, very well then. I hope here be truths.
Why, very well then. I hope these are truths.
This will last out a night in Russia / When nights are longest there. I'll take my leave, / And leave you to the hearing of the cause; / Hoping you'll find good cause to whip them all.
This will last as long as a night in Russia when the nights there are longest. I'll leave and let you hear the case, hoping you'll find good reason to whip them all.
I think no less. Good morrow to your lordship.
I expect so. Good day, your lordship.
Now, sir, come on. What was done to Elbow's wife, once more?
Now, sir, go on. What was done to Elbow's wife, once more?
Once, sir? There was nothing done to her once.
Once, sir? Nothing was done to her once.
I beseech you, sir, ask him what this man did to my wife.
I beg you, sir, ask him what this man did to my wife.
I beseech your honour, ask me.
I beg your honour, ask me.
Well, sir, what did this gentleman to her?
Well, sir, what did this gentleman do to her?
I beseech you, sir, look in this gentleman's face. Good Master Froth, / look upon his honour; 'tis for a good purpose.—Doth your honour mark / his face?
I beg you, sir, look at this gentleman's face. Good Master Froth, look at his honour; it's for a good reason. Does your honour notice his face?
Nay, I beseech you, mark it well.
No, I beg you, look at it carefully.
Doth your honour see any harm in his face?
Does your honour see any harm in his face?

I'll be supposed upon a book, his face is the worst thing about him. / Good, then, if his face be the worst thing about him, how could Master / Froth do the constable's wife any harm? I would know that of your / honour.

I'll swear on the Bible his face is the worst thing about him. Well then, if his face is the worst thing about him, how could Master Froth do the constable's wife any harm? I'd like your honour to tell me that.
He's in the right. Constable. What say you to it?
He has a point. Constable, what do you say to that?
First, an it like you, the house is a respected house; next, this is a / respected fellow; and his mistress is a respected woman.
First, if you please, the house is a respected (he means suspected) house; next, this is a respected fellow; and his mistress is a respected woman.
By this hand, sir, his wife is a more respected person than any of us / all.
I swear, sir, his wife is a more respected person than any of us.
Varlet, thou liest; thou liest, wicked varlet! The time is yet to come / that she was ever respected with man, woman, or child.
You villain, you lie! You lie, you wicked villain! The day has never come when she was respected with any man, woman or child.
Sir, she was respected with him before he married with her.
Sir, she was respected with him before he married her.
Which is the wiser here, Justice or Iniquity? Is this true?
Which is the wiser here, Justice or Iniquity? Is this true?

O thou caitiff! O thou varlet! O thou wicked Hannibal! I respected with / her before I was married to her? If ever I was respected with her, or / she with me, let not your worship think me the poor Duke's officer. / Prove this, thou wicked Hannibal, or I'll have mine action of battery / on thee.

Oh, you wretch! Oh, you villain! Oh, you wicked Hannibal (he means cannibal)! I respected with her before I married her? If I was ever respected with her, or she with me, don't let your worship think I'm the poor Duke's officer. Prove it, you wicked Hannibal, or I'll sue you for battery.
If he took you a box o' th' ear, you might have your action of slander / too.
If he gave you a box on the ear, you could sue him for slander as well.
Marry, I thank your good worship for it. What is't your worship's / pleasure I shall do with this wicked caitiff?
Why, thank you for that, your good worship. What would your worship like me to do with this wicked wretch?
Truly, officer, because he hath some offences in him that thou wouldst / discover if thou couldst, let him continue in his courses till thou / know'st what they are.
Honestly, officer, since he has some crimes in him that you would uncover if you could, let him carry on as he is until you find out what they are.
Marry, I thank your worship for it.—Thou seest, thou wicked varlet, / now, what's come upon thee. Thou art to continue now, thou varlet, thou / art to continue.
Why, thank you, your worship. (To Pompey) Now you see what has come down on you, you wicked villain. You are to continue now, you villain, you are to continue.
[To Froth] Where were you born, friend?
(To Froth) Where were you born, friend?
Are you of fourscore pounds a year?
Do you have eighty pounds a year?
So. [To Pompey] What trade are you of, sir?
I see. (To Pompey) And what's your trade, sir?
A tapster, a poor widow's tapster.
A barman, a poor widow's barman.
Hath she had any more than one husband?
Has she had more than one husband?
Nine, sir; Overdone by the last.
Nine, sir. She was Overdone by the last.

Nine?—Come hither to me, Master Froth. Master Froth, I would not have / you acquainted with tapsters; they will draw you, Master Froth, and you / will hang them. Get you gone, and let me hear no more of you.

Nine? Come over here, Master Froth. Master Froth, I'd rather you didn't mix with barmen. They will draw you in like beer, Master Froth, and you'll have them hanged. Off you go, and let me hear no more about you.
I thank your worship. For mine own part, I never come into any room in / a taphouse but I am drawn in.
Thank you, your worship. For my part, I never go into a room in a tavern without being drawn in.
Well, no more of it, Master Froth. Farewell.
Well, that's enough, Master Froth. Goodbye.
Come you hither to me, Master tapster. What's your name, Master / tapster?
Come over here, Master Barman. What's your name, Master Barman?

Troth, and your bum is the greatest thing about you; so that, in the / beastliest sense, you are Pompey the great. Pompey, you are partly a / bawd, Pompey, howsoever you colour it in being a tapster, are you not? / Come, tell me true, it shall be the better for you.

Honestly, your bum is the biggest thing about you, so in the crudest sense you are Pompey the Great. Pompey, you're partly a pimp, however you disguise it by being a barman, aren't you? Come on, tell me the truth; it will go better for you.
Truly, sir, I am a poor fellow that would live.
Honestly, sir, I'm a poor fellow trying to make a living.
How would you live, Pompey? By being a bawd? What do you think of the / trade, Pompey? Is it a lawful trade?
How do you make a living, Pompey? By being a pimp? What do you think of the trade, Pompey? Is it a lawful trade?
If the law would allow it, sir.
It would be, sir, if the law allowed it.
But the law will not allow it, Pompey; nor it shall not be allowed in / Vienna.
But the law won't allow it, Pompey, and it will not be allowed in Vienna.
Does your worship mean to geld and splay all the youth of the city?
Does your worship plan to castrate and spay all the young people in the city?
Truly, sir, in my poor opinion, they will to't then. If your worship / will take order for the drabs and the knaves, you need not to fear the / bawds.
Then honestly, sir, in my humble opinion, they'll go on doing it. If your worship deals with the whores and the rogues, you won't need to worry about the pimps.
There is pretty orders beginning, I can tell you. It is but heading and / hanging.
I can tell you, some fine orders are being made. It's nothing but beheading and hanging.

If you head and hang all that offend that way but for ten year / together, you'll be glad to give out a commission for more heads. If / this law hold in Vienna ten year, I'll rent the fairest house in it / after threepence a bay. If you live to see this come to pass, say / Pompey told you so.

If you behead and hang everyone who offends that way for ten years running, you'll be glad to send out an order for more heads. If this law lasts ten years in Vienna, I'll rent the finest house in it for threepence a room. If you live to see it, say Pompey told you so.

Thank you, good Pompey; and, in requital of your prophecy, hark you: I / advise you, let me not find you before me again upon any complaint / whatsoever; no, not for dwelling where you do. If I do, Pompey, I shall / beat you to your tent, and prove a shrewd Caesar to you. In plain / dealing, Pompey, I shall have you whipped. So for this time, Pompey, / fare you well.

Thank you, good Pompey. And in return for your prophecy, listen: I advise you not to let me find you before me again on any complaint at all, not even for living where you live. If I do, Pompey, I'll beat you back to your tent and be a harsh Caesar to you. To put it plainly, Pompey, I'll have you whipped. So for now, Pompey, goodbye.

I thank your worship for your good counsel. [Aside] But I shall / follow it as the flesh and fortune shall better determine. / Whip me? No, no; let carman whip his jade; / The valiant heart's not whipped out of his trade.

Thank you, your worship, for your good advice. (Aside) But I'll follow it as my body and my luck decide. Whip me? No, no. Let the carter whip his old nag; a brave heart can't be whipped out of his trade.
Come hither to me, Master Elbow. Come hither, Master Constable. How / long have you been in this place of constable?
Come here, Master Elbow. Come here, Master Constable. How long have you been a constable?
Seven year and a half, sir.
Seven and a half years, sir.
I thought, by the readiness in the office, you had continued in it / sometime. You say seven years together?
I thought, from how expert you are at the job, that you'd been doing it for some time. Seven years in a row, you say?
Alas, it hath been great pains to you. They do you wrong to put you so / oft upon't. Are there not men in your ward sufficient to serve it?
Oh dear, that must have been a great burden for you. It's unfair to make you do it so often. Aren't there men in your district able to serve?
Faith, sir, few of any wit in such matters. As they are chosen, they / are glad to choose me for them; I do it for some piece of money, and go / through with all.
Honestly, sir, few with any brains for such matters. When they are chosen, they're glad to choose me in their place. I do it for a bit of money and handle it all.
Look you bring me in the names of some six or seven, the most / sufficient of your parish.
Make sure you bring me the names of six or seven of the most capable men in your parish.
To my house. Fare you well.
What time do you think it is?
I pray you home to dinner with me.
Please come home and have lunch with me.
It grieves me for the death of Claudio, / But there's no remedy.
Claudio's death makes me sad, but there's nothing to be done.
It is but needful. / Mercy is not itself that oft looks so; / Pardon is still the nurse of second woe. / But yet, Poor Claudio! There's no remedy. / Come, sir.
It's only necessary. Mercy is not really mercy when it is shown too often; pardon always breeds a second wrong. And yet, poor Claudio! There's nothing to be done. Come, sir.
He's hearing of a cause. He will come straight. / I'll tell him of you.
He's hearing a case. He'll come in a moment. I'll tell him you're here.
I'll know / His pleasure, may be he will relent. Alas, / He hath but as offended in a dream; / All sects, all ages, smack of this vice, and he / To die for 't!
I'll find out what he wants; maybe he will relent. Oh, he has only sinned as if in a dream. People of every kind and every age have a taste of this vice, and he has to die for it!
Is it your will Claudio shall die tomorrow?
Is it your wish that Claudio should die tomorrow?
Did not I tell thee yea? Hadst thou not order? / Why dost thou ask again?
Didn't I tell you yes? Didn't you have your orders? Why are you asking again?
Lest I might be too rash. / Under your good correction, I have seen / When, after execution, judgement hath / Repented o'er his doom.
In case I might be acting too hastily. With respect, I have seen judges, after an execution, regret their sentence.
Go to; let that be mine. / Do you your office, or give up your place, / And you shall well be spared.
Enough; leave that to me. Do your job, or resign, and you won't be missed.
I crave your honour's pardon. / What shall be done, sir, with the groaning Juliet? / She's very near her hour.
I beg your honour's pardon. What is to be done, sir, with Juliet? She is groaning in labour; her time is very near.
Dispose of her / To some more fitter place; and that with speed.
Move her to some more suitable place, and quickly.
Here is the sister of the man condemned / Desires access to you.
The sister of the condemned man is here and asks to see you.
Ay, my good lord, a very virtuous maid, / And to be shortly of a sisterhood, / If not already.
Yes, my good lord, a very virtuous young woman who is soon to join a sisterhood, if she hasn't already.
See you the fornicatress be removed; / Let her have needful but not lavish means; / There shall be order for it.
See that the fornicator is moved. Give her what she needs, but nothing extravagant. Orders will be given for it.
(Starting to leave) God save your honour!
Stay a little while. [To Isabella] You are welcome. What's your / will?
Stay a little while. (To Isabella) You are welcome. What do you want?
I am a woeful suitor to your honour, / Please but your honour hear me.
I come to your honour with a sorrowful request, if your honour will only hear me.

There is a vice that most I do abhor, / And most desire should meet the blow of justice; / For which I would not plead, but that I must; / For which I must not plead, but that I am / At war 'twixt will and will not.

There is a vice that I hate above all others, and which I most want to see struck by justice. I would not plead for it, except that I must; I must not plead for it, except that I am torn between wanting to and not wanting to.
I have a brother is condemned to die; / I do beseech you, let it be his fault, / And not my brother.
I have a brother who is condemned to die. I beg you, let it be his crime that dies, and not my brother.
Heaven give you the grace to move him.

Condemn the fault, and not the actor of it? / Why, every fault's condemned ere it be done. / Mine were the very cipher of a function / To find the faults whose fine stands in record, / And let go by the actor.

Condemn the crime and not the man who did it? Why, every crime is condemned before it is committed. My job would be worth nothing if all I did was record the punishments for crimes and let the criminals go free.
O just but severe law! / I had a brother, then. Heaven keep your honour!
Oh, just but harsh law! Then I had a brother. Heaven keep your honour!

[To Isabella] Give't not o'er so. To him again, entreat him, / Kneel down before him, hang upon his gown; / You are too cold. If you should need a pin, / You could not with more tame a tongue desire it. / To him, I say.

(To Isabella) Don't give up like that. Go back to him, beg him, kneel down in front of him, cling to his robe. You're too cold. If you were asking for a pin, you couldn't ask more tamely. Go to him, I say.
Young lady, nothing can be done.
Yes, I do think that you might pardon him, / And neither heaven nor man grieve at the mercy.
Yes, I think you could pardon him, and neither heaven nor any man would be sorry for the mercy.
But can you if you would?
But could you, if you wanted to?
Look, what I will not, that I cannot do.
Listen: what I will not do, I cannot do.
But might you do't, and do the world no wrong, / If so your heart were touched with that remorse / As mine is to him?
But could you do it without doing the world any wrong, if your heart were touched with the same pity that mine feels for him?
He has been sentenced; it's too late.

Too late? Why, no. I that do speak a word / May call it back again. Well, believe this: / No ceremony that to great ones longs, / Not the king's crown, nor the deputed sword, / The marshal's truncheon, nor the judge's robe, / Become them with one half so good a grace / As mercy does. / If he had been as you, and you as he, / You would have slipped like him, but he like you / Would not have been so stern.

Too late? Why, no. I can speak a word and take it back again. So believe this: none of the trappings that belong to the great, not the king's crown, nor the sword of his deputy, nor the marshal's baton, nor the judge's robe, suits them half so gracefully as mercy does. If he had been in your place, and you in his, you would have slipped as he did; but he, in your place, would not have been so harsh.
I would to heaven I had your potency, / And you were Isabel! Should it then be thus? / No; I would tell what 'twere to be a judge / And what a prisoner.
I wish to heaven I had your power, and you were Isabel! Would it go like this then? No. I would show you what it means to be a judge, and what it means to be a prisoner.
[Aside] Ay, touch him; there's the vein.
(Aside) Yes, get at him; that's the spot.
Your brother is a forfeit of the law, / And you but waste your words.
Your brother's life is forfeit to the law, and you are only wasting your words.

Alas, alas! / Why, all the souls that were were forfeit once, / And He that might the vantage best have took / Found out the remedy. How would you be / If He, which is the top of judgement, should / But judge you as you are? O, think on that, / And mercy then will breathe within your lips, / Like man new made.

Oh, oh! Why, every soul that ever lived was once forfeit, and He who had every right to take advantage of that found a way to save them instead. What would become of you if He, the highest judge of all, judged you as you are? Oh, think about that, and then mercy will breathe from your lips, as if you were a man made new.
Be you content, fair maid. / It is the law, not I, condemns your brother. / Were he my kinsman, brother, or my son, / It should be thus with him. He must die tomorrow.
Calm yourself, lovely young woman. It is the law that condemns your brother, not me. If he were my relative, my brother or my son, it would be the same for him. He must die tomorrow.

Tomorrow? O, that's sudden! Spare him, spare him! / He's not prepared for death. Even for our kitchens / We kill the fowl of season. Shall we serve heaven / With less respect than we do minister / To our gross selves? Good, good my lord, bethink you. / Who is it that hath died for this offence? / There's many have committed it.

Tomorrow? Oh, that's so sudden! Spare him, spare him! He isn't ready to die. Even for our kitchens we only kill birds when they are in season. Shall we serve heaven with less care than we feed our own coarse bodies? My good, good lord, think again. Who has ever died for this crime? Plenty have committed it.

The law hath not been dead, though it hath slept. / Those many had not dared to do that evil / If the first that did th' edict infringe / Had answered for his deed. Now 'tis awake, / Takes note of what is done, and, like a prophet, / Looks in a glass that shows what future evils, / Either now, or by remissness new conceived, / And so in progress to be hatched and born, / Are now to have no successive degrees, / But, where they live, to end.

The law has not been dead, though it has been asleep. All those people would not have dared to do that wrong if the first person who broke the law had been made to answer for it. Now it is awake. It notices what is done and, like a prophet, looks into a crystal ball that shows future crimes, whether already planned or newly conceived through carelessness and so on their way to being hatched and born, and it means them to have no further stages, but to end where they are.

I show it most of all when I show justice; / For then I pity those I do not know, / Which a dismissed offence would after gall, / And do him right that, answering one foul wrong, / Lives not to act another. Be satisfied; / Your brother dies tomorrow; be content.

I show it most of all when I show justice. Then I pity people I don't know, who would later be hurt by a crime that went unpunished; and I do right by the man who pays for one foul crime and doesn't live to commit another. Be satisfied. Your brother dies tomorrow. Accept it.
So you must be the first that gives this sentence, / And he that suffers. O, it is excellent / To have a giant's strength; but it is tyrannous / To use it like a giant.
So you must be the first to pass this sentence, and he the first to suffer it. Oh, it is wonderful to have a giant's strength, but it is tyranny to use it like a giant.

Could great men thunder / As Jove himself does, Jove would ne'er be quiet, / For every pelting petty officer / Would use his heaven for thunder. / Nothing but thunder. Merciful Heaven, / Thou rather with thy sharp and sulphurous bolt / Splits the unwedgeable and gnarled oak, / Than the soft myrtle. But man, proud man, / Dressed in a little brief authority, / Most ignorant of what he's most assured, / His glassy essence, like an angry ape / Plays such fantastic tricks before high heaven / As makes the angels weep; who, with our spleens, / Would all themselves laugh mortal.

If great men could thunder like Jove himself, Jove would never have any peace, because every paltry little official would use his sky to thunder in. Nothing but thunder. Merciful heaven, you would rather split the gnarled oak that no wedge can split with your sharp, sulphurous lightning than the soft myrtle. But man, proud man, dressed up in a little brief authority, most ignorant of what he is most sure of, his own fragile soul, plays such crazy tricks before high heaven, like an angry ape, that he makes the angels weep; and if they had our tempers, they would laugh themselves to death.
O, to him, to him, wench! He will relent; / He's coming. I perceive 't.
Oh, at him, at him, girl! He will give in. He's coming round, I can see it.
Heaven grant she wins him over.
We cannot weigh our brother with ourself. / Great men may jest with saints; 'tis wit in them, / But in the less, foul profanation.
We cannot judge our brother by the same scale as ourselves. Great men may joke about saints; in them it is wit, but in lesser men it is foul blasphemy.
Thou'rt i' th' right, girl; more o' that.
You're right, girl. More of that.
That in the captain's but a choleric word / Which in the soldier is flat blasphemy.
What is only a hot-tempered word from the captain is downright blasphemy from the soldier.
Art advised o' that? More on't.
Do you know that? More of it.
Why do you put these sayings upon me?
Why do you apply these sayings to me?

Because authority, though it err like others, / Hath yet a kind of medicine in itself / That skins the vice o' th' top. Go to your bosom, / Knock there, and ask your heart what it doth know / That's like my brother's fault. If it confess / A natural guiltiness such as is his, / Let it not sound a thought upon your tongue / Against my brother's life.

Because authority, though it makes mistakes like anyone else, has a kind of medicine of its own that grows skin over the sore on top. Look into your own breast. Knock there and ask your heart if it knows anything like my brother's fault. If it admits a natural guilt like his, don't let it speak a single thought on your tongue against my brother's life.
She speaks, and 'tis such sense / That my sense breeds with it. [Going] / Fare you well.
She speaks such sense that my senses are stirred by it. (Starting to leave) Goodbye.
I will bethink me. Come again tomorrow.
I will think it over. Come back tomorrow.
Hark how I'll bribe you. Good my lord, turn back.
Listen to how I will bribe you. My good lord, turn back.
Ay, with such gifts that heaven shall share with you.
Yes, with gifts that heaven itself will share with you.
(To Isabella) Otherwise you'd have ruined everything.

Not with fond shekels of the tested gold, / Or stones, whose rates are either rich or poor / As fancy values them, but with true prayers, / That shall be up at heaven and enter there / Ere sunrise, prayers from preserved souls, / From fasting maids, whose minds are dedicate / To nothing temporal.

Not with silly coins of tested gold, or with gems whose value is high or low depending on fashion, but with true prayers that will rise to heaven and enter it before sunrise: prayers from souls kept pure, from fasting young women whose minds are devoted to nothing of this world.
[Aside to Isabella] Go to, 'tis well; away.
(Aside to Isabella) Good, that's done it. Let's go.
[Aside] Amen. / For I am that way going to temptation, / Where prayers cross.
(Aside) Amen. For I am heading towards temptation, where prayers cross each other.
At what hour tomorrow / Shall I attend your lordship?
At what time tomorrow shall I come to your lordship?

From thee, even from thy virtue! / What's this? What's this? Is this her fault or mine? / The tempter or the tempted, who sins most, ha? / Not she; nor doth she tempt; but it is I / That, lying by the violet in the sun, / Do as the carrion does, not as the flower, / Corrupt with virtuous season. Can it be / That modesty may more betray our sense / Than woman's lightness? Having waste ground enough, / Shall we desire to raze the sanctuary / And pitch our evils there? O, fie, fie, fie! / What dost thou, or what art thou, Angelo? / Dost thou desire her foully for those things / That make her good? O, let her brother live. / Thieves for their robbery have authority / When judges steal themselves. What, do I love her, / That I desire to hear her speak again / And feast upon her eyes? What is't I dream on? / O cunning enemy, that, to catch a saint, / With saints dost bait thy hook! Most dangerous / Is that temptation that doth goad us on / To sin in loving virtue. Never could the strumpet / With all her double vigour, art, and nature, / Once stir my temper, but this virtuous maid / Subdues me quite. Ever till now / When men were fond, I smiled and wondered how.

Safe from you, even from your virtue! What's this? What's this? Is it her fault or mine? Who sins more, the tempter or the tempted? Not her. She doesn't tempt me. It is I who, lying beside the violet in the sunshine, behave like the rotting carcass and not like the flower, and go bad in the same good season that makes it bloom. Can it be that modesty arouses our senses more than a woman's looseness? When there is plenty of waste ground, do we want to knock down the holy place and set up our sins there? Oh, shame, shame, shame! What are you doing, Angelo, and what are you? Do you desire her foully for the very things that make her good? Oh, let her brother live. Thieves have a licence to rob when judges steal themselves. What, do I love her, that I want to hear her speak again and feast my eyes on hers? What am I dreaming about? Oh cunning devil, who baits his hook with a saint to catch a saint! The most dangerous temptation is the one that drives us to sin through loving virtue. The whore, with all her double power of art and nature, could never once stir my passions, but this virtuous young woman conquers me completely. Until now, when men were lovesick, I smiled and wondered how they could be.
Hail to you, Provost, so I think you are.
Greetings to you, Provost; I think that's who you are.
I am the Provost. What's your will, good friar?
I am the Provost. What do you want, good friar?

Bound by my charity and my blessed order, / I come to visit the afflicted spirits / Here in the prison. Do me the common right / To let me see them, and to make me know / The nature of their crimes, that I may minister / To them accordingly.

Bound by charity and by my holy order, I have come to visit the troubled souls here in the prison. Grant me the usual right of seeing them, and tell me what their crimes are, so that I can minister to each one properly.
I would do more than that, if more were needful.
I would do more than that, if more were needed.

Look, here comes one, a gentlewoman of mine, / Who, falling in the flaws of her own youth, / Hath blistered her report. She is with child, / And he that got it, sentenced: a young man / More fit to do another such offence / Than die for this.

Look, here comes one, a young lady in my charge, who fell through the weaknesses of her youth and has scarred her good name. She is pregnant, and the man who fathered the child is sentenced: a young man more fit to commit the same offence again than to die for this one.
As I do think, tomorrow. / [To Juliet] I have provided for you; stay a while / And you shall be conducted.
Tomorrow, I believe. (To Juliet) I have made arrangements for you. Wait a while and you will be taken there.
Repent you, fair one, of the sin you carry?
Do you repent, lovely one, of the sin you are carrying?
I do; and bear the shame most patiently.
I do, and I bear the shame very patiently.
I'll teach you how you shall arraign your conscience, / And try your penitence, if it be sound / Or hollowly put on.
I will teach you how to put your conscience on trial and test your repentance, whether it is sound or just hollow show.
Love you the man that wronged you?
Do you love the man who wronged you?
Yes, as I love the woman that wronged him.
Yes, just as I love the woman who wronged him.
So then it seems your most offenceful act / Was mutually committed?
So it seems your sinful act was committed by both of you together?
Then was your sin of heavier kind than his.
Then your sin was heavier than his.
I do confess it, and repent it, father.
I confess it, and I repent it, father.

'Tis meet so, daughter; but lest you do repent / As that the sin hath brought you to this shame, / Which sorrow is always toward ourselves, not heaven, / Showing we would not spare heaven as we love it, / But as we stand in fear—

That is right, daughter. But in case you are repenting only because the sin has brought you to this shame, which is the kind of sorrow that is always for ourselves and not for heaven, and shows that we keep from offending heaven not because we love it but because we fear it...
I do repent me as it is an evil, / And take the shame with joy.
I repent because it is a sin, and I accept the shame with joy.
There rest. / Your partner, as I hear, must die tomorrow, / And I am going with instruction to him. / Grace go with you! Benedicite!
Keep to that. Your partner, I hear, must die tomorrow, and I am going to give him spiritual guidance. Grace go with you! God bless you!
Must die tomorrow? O, injurious love / That respites me a life, whose very comfort / Is still a dying horror!
Must die tomorrow? Oh, cruel love, that spares my life when the only comfort of that life is a constant, dying horror!

When I would pray and think, I think and pray / To several subjects. Heaven hath my empty words, / Whilst my invention, hearing not my tongue, / Anchors on Isabel. Heaven in my mouth, / As if I did but only chew his name, / And in my heart the strong and swelling evil / Of my conception. The state whereon I studied / Is, like a good thing being often read, / Grown sere and tedious; yea, my gravity, / Wherein—let no man hear me—I take pride, / Could I with boot change for an idle plume / Which the air beats for vain. O place, O form, / How often dost thou with thy case, thy habit, / Wrench awe from fools, and tie the wiser souls / To thy false seeming! Blood, thou art blood. / Let's write good angel on the devil's horn. / 'Tis not the devil's crest.

When I try to pray and think, my thoughts and prayers go to different places. Heaven gets my empty words, while my imagination, not listening to my tongue, is anchored on Isabel. Heaven is in my mouth, as if I were only chewing on its name, and in my heart is the strong and swelling evil of my desire. The government I used to study has grown dry and boring, like a good book read too often. Yes, even my seriousness, which, let no one hear me say it, I take pride in, I would gladly trade for a silly feather blown about by the wind. Oh rank, oh outward show, how often your mere outside and costume frighten fools into awe, and trap even wiser souls into believing your false appearance! Flesh, you are only flesh. Write "good angel" on the devil's horn, and it is no longer the devil's badge.
One Isabel, a sister, desires access to you.
A woman called Isabel, a nun, wants to see you.

O heavens, / Why does my blood thus muster to my heart, / Making both it unable for itself / And dispossessing all my other parts / Of necessary fitness? / So play the foolish throngs with one that swoons, / Come all to help him, and so stop the air / By which he should revive. And even so / The general subject to a well-wished king / Quit their own part, and in obsequious fondness / Crowd to his presence, where their untaught love / Must needs appear offence.

Oh heavens, why is my blood rushing to my heart like this, making it unable to work and robbing every other part of me of the strength it needs? This is how foolish crowds behave around someone who faints: they all come to help him and so block the air that would revive him. And in the same way the subjects of a well-loved king leave their own work and in fawning devotion crowd around him, where their clumsy love can only seem an offence.
I am come to know your pleasure.
I have come to hear what you have decided.
That you might know it, would much better please me / Than to demand what 'tis. Your brother cannot live.
I would be much better pleased if you knew it without having to ask. Your brother cannot live.
Even so. Heaven keep your honour.
I see. Heaven keep your honour.
Yet may he live a while. And, it may be, / As long as you or I. Yet he must die.
And yet he may live a while; perhaps as long as you or I. And yet he must die.
When, I beseech you? That in his reprieve, / Longer or shorter, he may be so fitted / That his soul sicken not.
When, I beg you? So that during his reprieve, however long or short, he can be made ready, and his soul does not go sick.

Ha! Fie, these filthy vices! It were as good / To pardon him that hath from nature stolen / A man already made, as to remit / Their saucy sweetness that do coin heaven's image / In stamps that are forbid. 'Tis all as easy / Falsely to take away a life true made / As to put metal in restrained means / To make a false one.

Ha! Shame on these filthy vices! It would be as right to pardon a man who has stolen from nature a person already made, by murder, as to excuse the insolent pleasure of those who stamp heaven's image on forbidden coins and make illegitimate children. It is just as easy wrongly to take away a lawfully made life as to pour metal into a banned mould to make a false one.
'Tis set down so in heaven, but not in earth.
That is how it is written in heaven, but not on earth.

Say you so? Then I shall pose you quickly. / Which had you rather, that the most just law / Now took your brother's life; or, to redeem him, / Give up your body to such sweet uncleanness / As she that he hath stained?

Do you say so? Then I will quickly put a question to you. Which would you rather: that the perfectly just law should now take your brother's life, or that, to buy him back, you should give your body up to the same sweet filth as the woman he has stained?
Sir, believe this: / I had rather give my body than my soul.
Sir, believe this: I would rather give up my body than my soul.
I talk not of your soul. Our compelled sins / Stand more for number than for accompt.
I am not talking about your soul. Sins we are forced into are counted, but not held against us.

Nay, I'll not warrant that, for I can speak / Against the thing I say. Answer to this: / I, now the voice of the recorded law, / Pronounce a sentence on your brother's life. / Might there not be a charity in sin / To save this brother's life?

No, I won't swear to that, because I could argue against what I've just said. Answer this. I, who am now the voice of the written law, pass sentence on your brother's life. Might there not be a kind of charity in a sin committed to save this brother's life?
Please you to do't, / I'll take it as a peril to my soul; / It is no sin at all, but charity.
If you are willing to do it, I'll take the risk to my soul. It isn't a sin at all, but charity.
Pleased you to do't at peril of your soul, / Were equal poise of sin and charity.
If you were willing to do it at the risk of your soul, the sin and the charity would balance out.

That I do beg his life, if it be sin, / Heaven let me bear it. You granting of my suit, / If that be sin, I'll make it my morn prayer / To have it added to the faults of mine, / And nothing of your answer.

If it is a sin for me to beg for his life, let heaven make me carry it. If it is a sin for you to grant my request, I will pray every morning to have it added to my own faults, and none of it charged to you.
Nay, but hear me. / Your sense pursues not mine. Either you are ignorant, / Or seem so, crafty; and that's not good.
No, listen to me. You are not following my meaning. Either you are ignorant, or you are cunningly pretending to be, and that is not good.
Let me be ignorant, and in nothing good, / But graciously to know I am no better.
Let me be ignorant, and good in nothing, except in knowing, by grace, that I am no better.
