Thus wisdom wishes to appear most bright / When it doth tax itself, as these black masks / Proclaim an enshield beauty ten times louder / Than beauty could, displayed. But mark me; / To be received plain, I'll speak more gross. / Your brother is to die.

That is how wisdom likes to shine most brightly, when it accuses itself, just as these black masks announce the hidden beauty behind them ten times more loudly than the beauty could if it were on show. But listen. To be understood plainly, I'll speak more crudely. Your brother is to die.
And his offence is so, as it appears, / Accountant to the law upon that pain.
And his crime, as it appears, makes him answerable to the law for that penalty.

Admit no other way to save his life— / As I subscribe not that, nor any other, / But, in the loss of question, that you, his sister, / Finding yourself desired of such a person / Whose credit with the judge, or own great place, / Could fetch your brother from the manacles / Of the all-binding law; and that there were / No earthly mean to save him but that either / You must lay down the treasures of your body / To this supposed, or else to let him suffer, / What would you do?

Suppose there is no other way to save his life (not that I agree to that, or to anything else; I am only putting it as a case for argument): suppose that you, his sister, found yourself desired by a man whose influence with the judge, or whose own high position, could free your brother from the chains of the law that binds everyone; and suppose there were no earthly way to save him except that either you give up the treasures of your body to this imagined man, or else let your brother suffer. What would you do?

As much for my poor brother as myself. / That is, were I under the terms of death, / Th' impression of keen whips I'd wear as rubies, / And strip myself to death as to a bed / That longing have been sick for, ere I'd yield / My body up to shame.

As much for my poor brother as for myself. That is, if I were under sentence of death, I would wear the marks of sharp whips like rubies, and strip for death as if for a bed I had been longing for, before I would give up my body to shame.
And 'twere the cheaper way. / Better it were a brother died at once / Than that a sister, by redeeming him, / Should die for ever.
And that would be the cheaper way. It is better for a brother to die once than for a sister, by saving him, to die for ever.
Were not you then as cruel as the sentence / That you have slandered so?
Wouldn't you then be as cruel as the sentence you have attacked so much?
Ignominy in ransom and free pardon / Are of two houses. Lawful mercy / Is nothing kin to foul redemption.
A disgraceful ransom and a free pardon come from two different families. Lawful mercy is no relation of foul bargaining.
You seemed of late to make the law a tyrant, / And rather proved the sliding of your brother / A merriment than a vice.
A moment ago you seemed to make the law a tyrant, and you made your brother's slip sound more like a bit of fun than a vice.
O, pardon me, my lord. It oft falls out, / To have what we would have, we speak not what we mean. / I something do excuse the thing I hate / For his advantage that I dearly love.
Oh, forgive me, my lord. It often happens that to get what we want, we don't say what we mean. I made some excuses for the thing I hate, for the sake of the brother I love dearly.
Else let my brother die, / If not a feodary but only he / Owe and succeed by weakness.
Then let my brother die, if he alone, and no one alongside him, owns and inherits this weakness.

Ay, as the glasses where they view themselves, / Which are as easy broke as they make forms. / Women?—Help, heaven! Men their creation mar / In profiting by them. Nay, call us ten times frail; / For we are soft as our complexions are, / And credulous to false prints.

Yes, like the mirrors they look at themselves in, which break as easily as they make images. Women! Heaven help us! Men spoil the creatures God made them by taking advantage of women. Yes, call us ten times weak, because we are as soft as our complexions, and easily take the stamp of false impressions.

I think it well. / And from this testimony of your own sex, / Since I suppose we are made to be no stronger / Than faults may shake our frames, let me be bold. / I do arrest your words. Be that you are, / That is, a woman. If you be more, you're none. / If you be one, as you are well expressed / By all external warrants, show it now / By putting on the destined livery.

I quite agree. And on this evidence from your own sex, since I suppose we are made no stronger than our faults can shake us, let me be bold. I take you at your word. Be what you are, that is, a woman. If you are more, you are not one. If you are one, as every outward sign shows you are, prove it now by putting on the uniform you were born to wear.
I have no tongue but one. Gentle my lord, / Let me intreat you speak the former language.
I have only one way of speaking. My kind lord, I beg you, talk the way you did before.
Understand it plainly: I love you.
My brother did love Juliet, / And you tell me that he shall die for 't.
My brother loved Juliet, and you tell me he must die for it.
He shall not, Isabel, if you give me love.
He will not, Isabel, if you give me your love.
I know your virtue hath a license in't, / Which seems a little fouler than it is, / To pluck on others.
I know your virtue allows itself a little freedom, which sounds fouler than it is, to test other people.
Believe me, on mine honour, / My words express my purpose.
Believe me, on my honour, my words mean what they say.

Ha! Little honour to be much believed, / And most pernicious purpose! Seeming, seeming! / I will proclaim thee, Angelo, look for't. / Sign me a present pardon for my brother / Or with an outstretched throat I'll tell the world aloud / What man thou art.

Ha! Not much honour to be believed, and a most wicked purpose! Show, all show! I will expose you, Angelo, wait and see. Sign me an immediate pardon for my brother, or I will tell the whole world at the top of my voice what kind of man you are.

Who will believe thee, Isabel? / My unsoiled name, th' austereness of my life, / My vouch against you, and my place i' th' state / Will so your accusation overweigh / That you shall stifle in your own report, / And smell of calumny. I have begun, / And now I give my sensual race the rein. / Fit thy consent to my sharp appetite; / Lay by all nicety and prolixious blushes / That banish what they sue for. Redeem thy brother / By yielding up thy body to my will; / Or else he must not only die the death, / But thy unkindness shall his death draw out / To ling'ring sufferance. Answer me tomorrow, / Or, by the affection that now guides me most, / I'll prove a tyrant to him. As for you, / Say what you can, my false o'erweighs your true.

Who will believe you, Isabel? My spotless name, the strictness of my life, my word against yours and my position in the state will so outweigh your accusation that you will choke on your own story, and it will stink of slander. I have started, and now I give my desire its head. Make your consent fit my sharp hunger. Put aside all your fussiness and long blushes that drive away what they really invite. Save your brother by giving your body to my will; or else he will not only die, but your unkindness will stretch his death out into lingering torture. Answer me tomorrow, or, by the passion that now rules me most, I will be a tyrant to him. As for you, say what you like: my lies outweigh your truth.

To whom should I complain? Did I tell this, / Who would believe me? O perilous mouths, / That bear in them one and the self-same tongue / Either of condemnation or approof, / Bidding the law make curtsy to their will, / Hooking both right and wrong to th' appetite, / To follow as it draws! I'll to my brother. / Though he hath fall'n by prompture of the blood, / Yet hath he in him such a mind of honour / That, had he twenty heads to tender down / On twenty bloody blocks, he'd yield them up / Before his sister should her body stoop / To such abhorred pollution. / Then, Isabel, live chaste, and, brother, die. / More than our brother is our chastity. / I'll tell him yet of Angelo's request, / And fit his mind to death, for his soul's rest.

Who can I complain to? If I told this, who would believe me? Oh, dangerous mouths, that keep one and the same tongue for condemning or approving, making the law bow to their will and hooking right and wrong alike onto their appetite, to follow wherever it pulls! I'll go to my brother. Though he fell through the urging of his blood, he has such a sense of honour that, if he had twenty heads to lay down on twenty bloody blocks, he would give them all up before his sister should lower her body to such hateful filth. Then, Isabel, live chaste, and, brother, die. Our chastity is worth more than our brother. Still, I'll tell him about Angelo's demand, and prepare his mind for death, so his soul can be at peace.
So then you hope of pardon from Lord Angelo?
So you hope for a pardon from Lord Angelo?
The miserable have no other medicine / But only hope. / I have hope to live, and am prepared to die.
The miserable have no other medicine but hope. I hope to live, and I am ready to die.

Be absolute for death. Either death or life / Shall thereby be the sweeter. Reason thus with life: / If I do lose thee, I do lose a thing / That none but fools would keep. A breath thou art, / Servile to all the skyey influences / That dost this habitation where thou keep'st / Hourly afflict. Merely, thou art death's fool; / For him thou labour'st by thy flight to shun, / And yet runn'st toward him still. Thou art not noble; / For all th' accommodations that thou bear'st / Are nursed by baseness. Thou'rt by no means valiant; / For thou dost fear the soft and tender fork / Of a poor worm. Thy best of rest is sleep, / And that thou oft provok'st, yet grossly fear'st / Thy death, which is no more. Thou art not thyself; / For thou exists on many a thousand grains / That issue out of dust. Happy thou art not; / For what thou hast not, still thou striv'st to get, / And what thou hast, forget'st. Thou art not certain; / For thy complexion shifts to strange effects / After the moon. If thou art rich, thou'rt poor; / For, like an ass whose back with ingots bows, / Thou bear'st thy heavy riches but a journey, / And death unloads thee. Friend hast thou none; / For thine own bowels which do call thee sire, / The mere effusion of thy proper loins, / Do curse the gout, serpigo, and the rheum / For ending thee no sooner. Thou hast nor youth nor age, / But as it were an after-dinner's sleep / Dreaming on both; for all thy blessed youth / Becomes as aged, and doth beg the alms / Of palsied eld; and when thou art old and rich, / Thou hast neither heat, affection, limb, nor beauty / To make thy riches pleasant. What's yet in this / That bears the name of life? Yet in this life / Lie hid more thousand deaths; yet death we fear, / That makes these odds all even.

Be completely ready for death. Then whichever comes, death or life, will be sweeter. Argue with life like this: if I lose you, I lose something only fools would want to keep. You are a breath, a slave to every influence of the stars that hour by hour afflicts this body you live in. You are simply death's fool, because you struggle to escape him by running, and still run towards him. You are not noble, because all the comforts you enjoy are fed by base things. You are not brave at all, because you fear the soft, delicate forked tongue of a poor worm. Your best rest is sleep, and you often seek it, yet you are terrified of death, which is no more than sleep. You are not your own self, because you are made of thousands of grains that come from dust. You are not happy, because you keep striving to get what you haven't got, and forget what you have. You are not constant, because your temperament changes in strange ways with the moon. If you are rich, you are poor; like a donkey whose back bends under gold bars, you carry your heavy wealth for only one journey, and then death unloads you. You have no friends, because your own children, who call you father, the very offspring of your body, curse gout, skin disease and catarrh for not finishing you off sooner. You have neither youth nor age, but only a kind of after-dinner nap dreaming of both. All your blessed youth lives like an old man and begs from shaky old age; and when you are old and rich, you have no warmth, no feeling, no strength and no beauty left to enjoy your riches. What is there in this that deserves the name of life? Yet in this life a thousand more deaths lie hidden; and still we fear death, which evens all these differences out.
I humbly thank you. / To sue to live, I find I seek to die, / And seeking death, find life. Let it come on.
Thank you humbly. I find that in begging to live I am seeking death, and in seeking death I find life. Let it come.
[Within] What ho! Peace here; grace and good company!
(Calling from outside) Hello! Peace be here, grace and good company!
Who's there? Come in. The wish deserves a welcome.
Who's there? Come in. That greeting deserves a welcome.
Dear sir, ere long I'll visit you again.
Dear sir, I will visit you again soon.
Most holy sir, I thank you.
My business is a word or two with Claudio.
My business is a word or two with Claudio.
And very welcome. Look, signior, here's your sister.
And you're very welcome. Look, signior, here's your sister.
Bring me to hear them speak, where I may be concealed.
Take me where I can hear them talk without being seen.
Now, sister, what comfort do you bring?

Why, / As all comforts are, most good, most good indeed. / Lord Angelo, having affairs to heaven, / Intends you for his swift ambassador, / Where you shall be an everlasting leiger. / Therefore your best appointment make with speed; / Tomorrow you set on.

Why, the best of comforts, the very best. Lord Angelo, having business with heaven, means to send you as his express ambassador, to stay there as a permanent envoy. So make your preparations quickly; you set off tomorrow.
None, but such remedy as, to save a head, / To cleave a heart in twain.
None, except one that would save a head by splitting a heart in two.
Yes, brother, you may live. / There is a devilish mercy in the judge, / If you'll implore it, that will free your life, / But fetter you till death.
Yes, brother, you could live. There is a devilish mercy in the judge which, if you beg for it, will set your life free but chain you until death.
Ay, just; perpetual durance; a restraint, / Though all the world's vastidity you had, / To a determined scope.
Yes, exactly, life imprisonment: a confinement to one fixed space, even if you had the whole wide world to roam.
In such a one as, you consenting to't, / Would bark your honour from that trunk you bear, / And leave you naked.
A kind that, if you agreed to it, would strip your honour from you like bark from a tree, and leave you naked.

O, I do fear thee, Claudio, and I quake, / Lest thou a feverous life shouldst entertain, / And six or seven winters more respect / Than a perpetual honour. Dar'st thou die? / The sense of death is most in apprehension; / And the poor beetle that we tread upon / In corporal sufferance finds a pang as great / As when a giant dies.

Oh, I'm afraid for you, Claudio, and I tremble in case you want to hang on to a feverish life, and value six or seven more winters above everlasting honour. Do you dare to die? The fear of death lies mostly in imagining it, and the poor beetle we tread on feels a pain in its body as great as a giant's when he dies.
Why give you me this shame? / Think you I can a resolution fetch / From flowery tenderness? If I must die, / I will encounter darkness as a bride / And hug it in mine arms.
Why do you shame me like this? Do you think I can get courage from flowery, soft words? If I must die, I will meet darkness like a bride and hug it in my arms.

There spake my brother! There my father's grave / Did utter forth a voice. Yes, thou must die. / Thou art too noble to conserve a life / In base appliances. This outward-sainted deputy, / Whose settled visage and deliberate word / Nips youth i' th' head, and follies doth enew / As falcon doth the fowl, is yet a devil. / His filth within being cast, he would appear / A pond as deep as hell.

That was my brother speaking! That was a voice from my father's grave. Yes, you must die. You are too noble to keep your life by low means. This deputy, a saint on the outside, whose fixed expression and careful words nip youth in the bud and drive follies into hiding as a falcon drives birds into the water, is still a devil. If the filth inside him were dredged out, he would look like a pond as deep as hell.
O, 'tis the cunning livery of hell / The damned'st body to invest and cover / In precise guards! Dost thou think, Claudio, / If I would yield him my virginity / Thou mightst be freed?
Oh, it is hell's cunning uniform, to dress and cover the most damned body in strict trimmings! Do you think, Claudio, that if I gave him my virginity, you might be set free?
Yes, he would give it thee, from this rank offence, / So to offend him still. This night's the time / That I should do what I abhor to name, / Or else thou diest tomorrow.
Yes, he would give you this foul crime as a licence, so you could go on committing it. Tonight is the time when I must do what I can't bear to name, or else you die tomorrow.
O, were it but my life, / I'd throw it down for your deliverance / As frankly as a pin.
Oh, if it were only my life, I'd throw it away to set you free as readily as a pin.
Be ready, Claudio, for your death tomorrow.
Be ready, Claudio, for your death tomorrow.
Yes. Has he affections in him / That thus can make him bite the law by th' nose / When he would force it? Sure it is no sin; / Or of the deadly seven it is the least.
Yes. Does he have passions in him that can make him tweak the law's nose when he means to enforce it? Surely it is no sin, or of the seven deadly sins it is the least.
If it were damnable, he being so wise, / Why would he for the momentary trick / Be perdurably fined? O Isabel!
If it were damnable, why would he, being so wise, risk everlasting punishment for a moment's pleasure? Oh, Isabel!
And a life of shame is a hateful one.

Ay, but to die, and go we know not where; / To lie in cold obstruction, and to rot; / This sensible warm motion to become / A kneaded clod; and the delighted spirit / To bathe in fiery floods, or to reside / In thrilling regions of thick-ribbed ice; / To be imprisoned in the viewless winds / And blown with restless violence round about / The pendent world; or to be worse than worst / Of those that lawless and incertain thought / Imagine howling—'tis too horrible. / The weariest and most loathed worldly life / That age, ache, penury, and imprisonment / Can lay on nature is a paradise / To what we fear of death.

Yes, but to die and go we don't know where; to lie cold and stiff and rot; for this warm, feeling, moving body to become a lump of clay; and for the spirit that once delighted to bathe in floods of fire, or live in freezing regions of thick walls of ice; to be imprisoned in the invisible winds and blown with restless violence round and round the hanging earth; or to be worse than the worst of those that wild, uncertain imagination pictures howling: it is too horrible. The most weary and hated life on earth that old age, pain, poverty and prison can lay on us is paradise compared with what we fear in death.
Sweet sister, let me live. / What sin you do to save a brother's life, / Nature dispenses with the deed so far / That it becomes a virtue.
Sweet sister, let me live. Whatever sin you commit to save a brother's life, nature excuses the act so far that it becomes a virtue.

O, you beast! / O faithless coward! O dishonest wretch! / Wilt thou be made a man out of my vice? / Is't not a kind of incest to take life / From thine own sister's shame? What should I think? / Heaven shield my mother played my father fair, / For such a warped slip of wilderness / Ne'er issued from his blood. Take my defiance, / Die, perish! Might but my bending down / Reprieve thee from thy fate, it should proceed. / I'll pray a thousand prayers for thy death, / No word to save thee.

Oh, you beast! Oh, faithless coward! Oh, dishonourable wretch! Will you be made a man out of my sin? Isn't it a kind of incest to take your life from your own sister's shame? What am I to think? Heaven grant my mother was faithful to my father, because such a twisted, wild offshoot never came from his blood. I reject you. Die, perish! If just my bending down could save you from your fate, I would let it go ahead. I'll pray a thousand prayers for your death and not one word to save you.
O fie, fie, fie! / Thy sin's not accidental, but a trade. / Mercy to thee would prove itself a bawd. / 'Tis best that thou diest quickly.
Oh, shame, shame, shame! Your sin is not an accident but a trade. Mercy to you would turn out to be a pimp. It's best that you die quickly.
Vouchsafe a word, young sister, but one word.
Allow me a word, young sister, just one word.
Might you dispense with your leisure, I would by and by have some / speech with you. The satisfaction I would require is likewise your own / benefit.
If you can spare the time, I would like to speak with you shortly. What I want from you will also be to your own benefit.
I have no superfluous leisure, my stay must be stolen out of other / affairs, but I will attend you a while.
I have no time to spare; anything I stay for has to be stolen from other business. But I will wait for you a while.

[To Claudio aside] Son, I have overheard what hath passed between / you and your sister. Angelo had never the purpose to corrupt her; only / he hath made an assay of her virtue, to practise his judgement with the / disposition of natures. She, having the truth of honour in her, hath / made him that gracious denial which he is most glad to receive. I am / confessor to Angelo, and I know this to be true; therefore prepare / yourself to death. Do not satisfy your resolution with hopes that are / fallible. Tomorrow you must die; go to your knees and make ready.

(Aside to Claudio) My son, I have overheard what passed between you and your sister. Angelo never meant to corrupt her. He was only testing her virtue, to practise his judgment of human nature. She, having true honour in her, gave him the gracious refusal he was very glad to receive. I am Angelo's confessor, and I know this is true. So prepare yourself for death. Don't comfort your resolve with hopes that will fail you. Tomorrow you must die. Go down on your knees and get ready.
Let me ask my sister pardon. I am so out of love with life that I will / sue to be rid of it.
Let me ask my sister's forgiveness. I am so out of love with life that I will beg to be rid of it.
That, now you are come, you will be gone. Leave me a while with the / maid; my mind promises with my habit no loss shall touch her by my / company.
That, now you have come, you will go. Leave me alone with the young woman for a while. My intentions, and my habit, promise that no harm will come to her in my company.

The hand that hath made you fair hath made you good. The goodness that / is cheap in beauty makes beauty brief in goodness; but grace, being the / soul of your complexion, shall keep the body of it ever fair. The / assault that Angelo hath made to you, fortune hath conveyed to my / understanding; and, but that frailty hath examples for his falling, I / should wonder at Angelo. How will you do to content this substitute, / and to save your brother?

The hand that made you beautiful has made you good. Goodness that holds beauty cheap soon makes the beauty lose its goodness; but grace, being the soul of your nature, will keep your outward self always beautiful. Chance has let me know of the assault Angelo has made on you, and if weakness did not have so many examples of falling like his, I would be amazed at Angelo. What will you do to satisfy this deputy and save your brother?

I am now going to resolve him. I had rather my brother die by the law / than my son should be unlawfully born. But, O, how much is the good / Duke deceived in Angelo! If ever he return, and I can speak to him, I / will open my lips in vain, or discover his government.

I am going now to give him my answer. I would rather my brother died lawfully than that a son of mine should be born unlawfully. But oh, how badly the good Duke has been deceived in Angelo! If he ever comes back and I can speak to him, I will either be wasting my breath or I will expose how Angelo has governed.

That shall not be much amiss. Yet, as the matter now stands, he will / avoid your accusation: he made trial of you only. Therefore fasten your / ear on my advisings, to the love I have in doing good, a remedy / presents itself. I do make myself believe that you may most / uprighteously do a poor wronged lady a merited benefit; redeem your / brother from the angry law; do no stain to your own gracious person; / and much please the absent Duke, if peradventure he shall ever return / to have hearing of this business.

That would not be a bad thing. But as things stand now, he will dodge your accusation by saying he was only testing you. So listen carefully to my advice. Out of my love of doing good, a remedy suggests itself. I truly believe you can, with complete integrity, do a poor, wronged lady a deserved favour, save your brother from the angry law, keep your own gracious self unstained, and greatly please the absent Duke, if by chance he ever returns to hear about this business.
Let me hear you speak farther. I have spirit to do anything that / appears not foul in the truth of my spirit.
Tell me more. I have the courage to do anything that does not seem foul to my conscience.
Virtue is bold, and goodness never fearful. Have you not heard speak of / Mariana, the sister of Frederick, the great soldier who miscarried at / sea?
Virtue is bold, and goodness never afraid. Have you heard of Mariana, the sister of Frederick, the great soldier who was lost at sea?
I have heard of the lady, and good words went with her name.
I have heard of the lady, and people always spoke well of her.

She should this Angelo have married, was affianced to her oath, and the / nuptial appointed. Between which time of the contract and limit of the / solemnity, her brother Frederick was wrecked at sea, having in that / perished vessel the dowry of his sister. But mark how heavily this / befell to the poor gentlewoman. There she lost a noble and renowned / brother, in his love toward her ever most kind and natural; with him, / the portion and sinew of her fortune, her marriage dowry; with both, / her combinate husband, this well-seeming Angelo.

Angelo was supposed to marry her. He was formally engaged to her under oath, and the wedding day was fixed. Between the contract and the ceremony her brother Frederick was shipwrecked, and her dowry went down with him in that ship. Think how hard this was for the poor lady. She lost a noble, famous brother who had always loved her dearly; with him she lost her fortune, her dowry; and with both she lost her promised husband, this respectable-looking Angelo.
Can this be so? Did Angelo so leave her?
Can this be true? Did Angelo really leave her like that?

Left her in her tears, and dried not one of them with his comfort, / swallowed his vows whole, pretending in her discoveries of dishonour; / in few, bestowed her on her own lamentation, which she yet wears for / his sake; and he, a marble to her tears, is washed with them, but / relents not.

He left her in tears and did not dry a single one of them with comfort. He swallowed his vows whole, claiming he had found she was dishonoured. In short, he left her to her grief, which she still wears for his sake; and he, like marble in the rain, is washed by her tears but never softens.
What a merit were it in death to take this poor maid from the world! / What corruption in this life, that it will let this man live! But how / out of this can she avail?
How good it would be of death to take this poor woman out of the world! And how corrupt this life is, to let this man live! But how can she gain anything from this?
It is a rupture that you may easily heal, and the cure of it not only / saves your brother, but keeps you from dishonour in doing it.
It is a break you can easily mend, and mending it not only saves your brother but keeps you from dishonour in doing so.

This forenamed maid hath yet in her the continuance of her first / affection. His unjust unkindness, that in all reason should have / quenched her love, hath, like an impediment in the current, made it / more violent and unruly. Go you to Angelo; answer his requiring with a / plausible obedience; agree with his demands to the point. Only refer / yourself to this advantage: first, that your stay with him may not be / long; that the time may have all shadow and silence in it; and the / place answer to convenience. This being granted in course, and now / follows all. We shall advise this wronged maid to stead up your / appointment, go in your place. If the encounter acknowledge itself / hereafter, it may compel him to her recompense; and here, by this, is / your brother saved, your honour untainted, the poor Mariana advantaged, / and the corrupt deputy scaled. The maid will I frame and make fit for / his attempt. If you think well to carry this as you may, the doubleness / of the benefit defends the deceit from reproof. What think you of it?

This woman I mentioned still feels the love she first felt. His unjust cruelty, which by rights should have killed her love, has instead, like a dam in a stream, made it stronger and wilder. Go to Angelo. Answer his demand with convincing obedience and agree to everything he asks. Only make these conditions: first, that you do not stay with him long; that the meeting happens in darkness and silence; and that the place is convenient. Once that is agreed, everything follows. We will advise this wronged woman to keep your appointment and go in your place. If the meeting comes out later, it may force him to make amends to her. And in this way your brother is saved, your honour kept clean, poor Mariana helped, and the corrupt deputy weighed and found wanting. I will prepare the woman and make her ready for his advances. If you are willing to carry this out, the double good it does will protect the trick from blame. What do you think?
The image of it gives me content already, and I trust it will grow to a / most prosperous perfection.
Just picturing it makes me happy already, and I trust it will turn out very successfully.

It lies much in your holding up. Haste you speedily to Angelo; if for / this night he entreat you to his bed, give him promise of satisfaction. / I will presently to Saint Luke's; there at the moated grange resides / this dejected Mariana. At that place call upon me; and dispatch with / Angelo, that it may be quickly.

Much depends on how well you play your part. Hurry to Angelo. If he asks you to come to his bed tonight, promise to satisfy him. I will go at once to Saint Luke's; there, at the moated farmhouse, this unhappy Mariana lives. Come and find me there, and settle things with Angelo quickly.
I thank you for this comfort. Fare you well, good father.
Thank you for this comfort. Goodbye, good father.
Nay, if there be no remedy for it, but that you will needs buy and sell / men and women like beasts, we shall have all the world drink brown and / white bastard.
No, if nothing can be done about it, and you insist on buying and selling men and women like animals, the whole world will be drinking brown and white bastard (a sweet wine).
O heavens, what stuff is here?
Oh heavens, what nonsense is this?

'Twas never merry world since, of two usuries, the merriest was put / down, and the worser allowed by order of law a furred gown to keep him / warm; and furred with fox on lambskins too, to signify that craft, / being richer than innocency, stands for the facing.

The world has never been merry since, of the two kinds of usury, the merriest was banned and the worse was allowed by law to wear a furred gown to keep it warm; and furred with fox on lambskin too, to show that cunning, being richer than innocence, makes the trimming.
Come your way, sir.—Bless you, good father friar.
Come along, sir. God bless you, good father friar.
And you, good brother father. What offence hath this man made you, sir?
And you, good brother father. What crime has this man committed, sir?
Marry, sir, he hath offended the law; and, sir, we take him to be a / thief too, sir; for we have found upon him, sir, a strange picklock, / which we have sent to the deputy.
Why, sir, he has broken the law. And, sir, we think he's a thief too, sir, because we found a strange lock-pick on him, sir, which we have sent to the deputy.

Fie, sirrah, a bawd, a wicked bawd; / The evil that thou causest to be done, / That is thy means to live. Do thou but think / What 'tis to cram a maw or clothe a back / From such a filthy vice. Say to thyself, / From their abominable and beastly touches / I drink, I eat, array myself, and live. / Canst thou believe thy living is a life, / So stinkingly depending? Go mend, go mend.

Shame on you, a pimp, a wicked pimp! The evil you cause to be done is how you make your living. Just think what it means to fill your belly or clothe your back from such a filthy vice. Say to yourself, "From their disgusting, beastly gropings I drink, I eat, I dress and I live." Can you believe your living is a life when it depends on such stink? Go and reform, go and reform.
Indeed, it does stink in some sort, sir. But yet, sir, I would prove—
It does stink in a way, sir, I admit. But still, sir, I would prove...
Nay, if the devil have given thee proofs for sin, / Thou wilt prove his. Take him to prison, officer. / Correction and instruction must both work / Ere this rude beast will profit.

No, if the devil has given you arguments to defend sin, you will prove to be his. Take him to prison, officer. Punishment and teaching must both work on this rough beast before he gets any good from them.
He must before the deputy, sir; he has given him warning. The deputy / cannot abide a whoremaster. If he be a whoremonger and comes before / him, he were as good go a mile on his errand.
He has to go before the deputy, sir; he has been warned. The deputy can't stand a whoremaster. If a whoremonger comes before him, he'd do better to go a mile out of his way.
That we were all, as some would seem to be, / Free from our faults, as faults from seeming, free!
If only we were all what some people seem to be, free from faults; or that faults were free from disguising themselves!
His neck will come to your waist—a cord, sir.
His neck will be like your waist: tied with a cord, sir.
I spy comfort, I cry bail! Here's a gentleman, and a friend of mine.
I see help! I call for bail! Here's a gentleman, and a friend of mine.

How now, noble Pompey? What, at the wheels of Caesar? Art thou led in / triumph? What, is there none of Pygmalion's images, newly made woman, / to be had now, for putting the hand in the pocket and extracting it / clutched? What reply, ha? What say'st thou to this tune, matter, and / method? Is't not drowned i' th' last rain, ha? What say'st thou, trot? / Is the world as it was, man? Which is the way? Is it sad and few words? / Or how? The trick of it?

Well now, noble Pompey? What, tied to Caesar's chariot wheels? Being led in triumph? What, are there no statues like Pygmalion's, just turned into women, to be had now by putting your hand in your pocket and pulling it out full of cash? What do you say? What do you think of this song, this business, this style? Has it drowned in the last rainstorm? What do you say, old woman? Is the world the way it was, man? What's the fashion? Is it gloomy and quiet? Or what? How does it go?
Still thus, and thus; still worse!
How doth my dear morsel, thy mistress? Procures she still, ha?
How is my dear little morsel, your mistress? Is she still procuring?
Troth, sir, she hath eaten up all her beef, and she is herself in the / tub.
Honestly, sir, she has eaten all her beef, and now she's in the tub herself (taking the sweating cure for disease).
Why, 'tis good. It is the right of it. It must be so. Ever your fresh / whore and your powdered bawd; an unshunned consequence; it must be so. / Art going to prison, Pompey?
Why, good. That's right. It has to be like that. Always your fresh whore and your salted bawd; it's unavoidable; it has to be like that. Are you going to prison, Pompey?
Why, 'tis not amiss, Pompey. Farewell. Go, say I sent thee thither. For / debt, Pompey? Or how?
Why, that's not a bad thing, Pompey. Goodbye. Go and say I sent you there. For debt, Pompey? Or what?
For being a bawd, for being a bawd.
For being a pimp, for being a pimp.

Well, then, imprison him. If imprisonment be the due of a bawd, why, / 'tis his right. Bawd is he doubtless, and of antiquity, too. Bawd born. / Farewell, good Pompey. Commend me to the prison, Pompey. You will turn / good husband now, Pompey; you will keep the house.

Well then, lock him up. If prison is what a pimp deserves, why, he's got his rights. He's a pimp, no doubt about it, and from an old family too. A born pimp. Goodbye, good Pompey. Give my regards to the prison, Pompey. You'll be a good householder now, Pompey; you'll stay at home.
I hope, sir, your good worship will be my bail.
I hope, sir, your good worship will put up my bail.

No, indeed, will I not, Pompey; it is not the wear. I will pray, / Pompey, to increase your bondage. If you take it not patiently, why, / your mettle is the more. Adieu, trusty Pompey.—Bless you, friar.

No, I certainly won't, Pompey. It isn't the fashion. I'll pray, Pompey, for your sentence to be made longer. If you don't take it patiently, why, you'll show all the more spirit. Goodbye, faithful Pompey. God bless you, friar.
Does Bridget paint still, Pompey, ha?
Does Bridget still paint her face, Pompey, eh?
You will not bail me then, sir?
So you won't bail me, sir?
Then, Pompey, nor now.—What news abroad, friar? What news?
Not then, Pompey, and not now. What's the news out there, friar? What news?
Off to your kennel, Pompey, go.
What news, friar, of the Duke?
What news, friar, of the Duke?
I know none. Can you tell me of any?
I don't know any. Can you tell me some?
Some say he is with the Emperor of Russia; other some, he is in Rome. / But where is he, think you?
Some say he's with the Emperor of Russia; others say he's in Rome. But where do you think he is?
I know not where, but wheresoever, I wish him well.
I don't know where, but wherever he is, I wish him well.
It was a mad fantastical trick of him to steal from the state and usurp / the beggary he was never born to. Lord Angelo dukes it well in his / absence. He puts transgression to't.
It was a crazy, fanciful trick of his to sneak away from the state and take up a beggar's life he was never born to. Lord Angelo plays the duke well while he's away. He comes down hard on wrongdoing.
A little more lenity to lechery would do no harm in him. Something too / crabbed that way, friar.
A bit more leniency towards lechery wouldn't hurt him. He's a bit too sour in that department, friar.
It is too general a vice, and severity must cure it.
It is too widespread a vice, and severity must cure it.

Yes, in good sooth, the vice is of a great kindred; it is well allied; / but it is impossible to extirp it quite, friar, till eating and / drinking be put down. They say this Angelo was not made by man and / woman after this downright way of creation. Is it true, think you?

Yes, honestly, the vice has a big family; it is well connected. But it is impossible to root it out completely, friar, until eating and drinking are banned. They say this Angelo wasn't made by a man and a woman in the usual straightforward way of creation. Do you think it's true?
How should he be made, then?

Some report a sea-maid spawned him; some, that he was begot between two / stockfishes. But it is certain that when he makes water, his urine is / congealed ice; that I know to be true. And he is a motion ungenerative; / that's infallible.

Some say a mermaid spawned him; some that he was fathered between two dried cod. But it's certain that when he pisses, his urine is frozen ice; I know that's true. And he's a puppet that can't breed; that's certain.
You are pleasant, sir, and speak apace.
You are amusing, sir, and you talk fast.

Why, what a ruthless thing is this in him, for the rebellion of a / codpiece to take away the life of a man! Would the Duke that is absent / have done this? Ere he would have hanged a man for the getting a / hundred bastards, he would have paid for the nursing a thousand. He had / some feeling of the sport; he knew the service, and that instructed him / to mercy.

Why, how heartless of him, to take a man's life because his codpiece rebelled! Would the absent Duke have done this? Before he hanged a man for fathering a hundred bastards, he'd have paid to nurse a thousand. He had some feeling for the sport. He knew the game, and that taught him mercy.
I never heard the absent Duke much detected for women; he was not / inclined that way.
I never heard that the absent Duke was much accused over women. He wasn't that way inclined.
Who, not the Duke? Yes, your beggar of fifty; and his use was to put a / ducat in her clack-dish. The Duke had crotchets in him. He would be / drunk too, that let me inform you.
What, not the Duke? Yes, with a beggar woman of fifty. And his habit was to drop a ducat in her begging bowl. The Duke had his quirks. He'd get drunk too, let me tell you.
Sir, I was an inward of his. A shy fellow was the Duke; and I believe I / know the cause of his withdrawing.
Sir, I was one of his close friends. The Duke was a secretive fellow, and I think I know why he went away.
What, I prithee, might be the cause?
What, please, might the reason be?
No, pardon. 'Tis a secret must be locked within the teeth and the lips. / But this I can let you understand: the greater file of the subject held / the Duke to be wise.
No, forgive me. It's a secret that must stay locked behind the teeth and lips. But I can tell you this much: most of his subjects thought the Duke was wise.
Wise? Why, no question but he was.
Wise? Why, there's no question he was.
A very superficial, ignorant, unweighing fellow.
A very shallow, ignorant, thoughtless fellow.

Either this is envy in you, folly, or mistaking. The very stream of his / life, and the business he hath helmed, must upon a warranted need give / him a better proclamation. Let him be but testimonied in his own / bringings-forth, and he shall appear to the envious a scholar, a / statesman, and a soldier. Therefore you speak unskilfully. Or, if your / knowledge be more, it is much darkened in your malice.

This is either envy in you, or foolishness, or a mistake. The whole course of his life and the business he has steered must, if they were properly examined, give him a better reputation. Judge him only by what he has done, and even the envious will see a scholar, a statesman and a soldier. So you speak without knowledge; or, if you know more, your malice has darkened it badly.
Sir, I know him, and I love him.
Sir, I know him, and I love him.
Love talks with better knowledge, and knowledge with dearer love.
Love speaks with better knowledge, and knowledge with deeper love.
Come, sir, I know what I know.
Come, sir, I know what I know.

I can hardly believe that, since you know not what you speak. But, if / ever the Duke return, as our prayers are he may, let me desire you to / make your answer before him. If it be honest you have spoke, you have / courage to maintain it. I am bound to call upon you, and I pray you / your name?

I can hardly believe that, since you don't know what you're saying. But if the Duke ever returns, as we pray he will, I ask you to answer for this in front of him. If you have spoken honestly, you'll have the courage to stand by it. I am duty bound to call on you. What is your name, please?
Sir, my name is Lucio, well known to the Duke.
Sir, my name is Lucio, well known to the Duke.
He shall know you better, sir, if I may live to report you.
He shall know you better, sir, if I live to report you.
O, you hope the Duke will return no more; or you imagine me too / unhurtful an opposite. But indeed, I can do you little harm. You'll / forswear this again.
Oh, you hope the Duke won't come back, or you think I'm too harmless an opponent. And in truth I can do you little harm. You'll deny all this later.
I'll be hanged first! Thou art deceived in me, friar. But no more of / this. Canst thou tell if Claudio die tomorrow or no?
I'll be hanged first! You've got me wrong, friar. But enough of this. Can you tell me whether Claudio dies tomorrow or not?

Why? For filling a bottle with a tun-dish. I would the Duke we talk of / were returned again. This ungenitured agent will unpeople the province / with continency. Sparrows must not build in his house-eaves because / they are lecherous. The Duke yet would have dark deeds darkly answered. / He would never bring them to light. Would he were returned! Marry, this / Claudio is condemned for untrussing. Farewell, good friar, I prithee / pray for me. The Duke, I say to thee again, would eat mutton on / Fridays. He's now past it; yet, and, I say to thee, he would mouth with / a beggar though she smelt brown bread and garlic. Say that I said so. / Farewell.

Why? For filling a bottle with a funnel. I wish the Duke we're talking about would come back. This sexless deputy will empty the province with his chastity. Sparrows won't be allowed to nest under his eaves because they're lecherous. The Duke would have had dark deeds dealt with in the dark; he'd never have dragged them into the light. I wish he'd come back! Why, this Claudio is condemned for undoing his breeches. Goodbye, good friar; please pray for me. The Duke, I tell you again, would eat mutton (loose women) on Fridays. He's past it now; and yet, I tell you, he'd kiss a beggar woman even if she stank of brown bread and garlic. Say I said so. Goodbye.
No might nor greatness in mortality / Can censure 'scape. Back-wounding calumny / The whitest virtue strikes. What king so strong / Can tie the gall up in the slanderous tongue? / But who comes here?

No power or greatness in this world can escape criticism. Slander that stabs in the back strikes even the purest virtue. What king is strong enough to tie up the poison in a slanderous tongue? But who is coming?
Go, away with her to prison.
Go on, take her away to prison.
Good my lord, be good to me. Your honour is accounted a merciful man, / good my lord.
My good lord, be kind to me. Your honour is thought to be a merciful man, my good lord.
Double and treble admonition, and still forfeit in the same kind? This / would make mercy swear and play the tyrant.
Warned twice and three times, and still guilty of the same offence? This would make mercy swear and act the tyrant.
A bawd of eleven years' continuance, may it please your honour.
She has been a madam for eleven years, if it please your honour.

My lord, this is one Lucio's information against me. Mistress Kate / Keepdown was with child by him in the Duke's time; he promised her / marriage. His child is a year and a quarter old come Philip and Jacob. / I have kept it myself; and see how he goes about to abuse me.

My lord, this is that Lucio informing against me. Mistress Kate Keepdown was pregnant by him in the Duke's time; he promised to marry her. His child will be a year and a quarter old on the first of May. I have looked after it myself, and look how he sets about ruining me.
That fellow is a fellow of much license. Let him be called before us. / Away with her to prison. Go to, no more words.
That fellow takes a lot of liberties. Have him called before us. Take her away to prison. Go on, not another word.

Provost, my brother Angelo will not be altered; Claudio must die / tomorrow. Let him be furnished with divines, and have all charitable / preparation. If my brother wrought by my pity, it should not be so with / him.

Provost, my colleague Angelo will not change his mind. Claudio must die tomorrow. Give him priests and every charitable preparation. If my colleague acted with my pity, it would not be like this for him.
So please you, this friar hath been with him, and advised him for th' / entertainment of death.
If you please, this friar has been with him and advised him how to meet death.
Not of this country, though my chance is now / To use it for my time. I am a brother / Of gracious order, late come from the See / In special business from his Holiness.
Not from this country, though I happen now to be staying here for a time. I am a brother of a holy order, recently arrived from the Pope's court on special business for his Holiness.
What news abroad i' th' world?
What news is there out in the world?

None, but that there is so great a fever on goodness that the / dissolution of it must cure it. Novelty is only in request, and as it / is as dangerous to be aged in any kind of course as it is virtuous to / be constant in any undertaking. There is scarce truth enough alive to / make societies secure; but security enough to make fellowships / accursed. Much upon this riddle runs the wisdom of the world. This news / is old enough, yet it is every day's news. I pray you, sir, of what / disposition was the Duke?

None, except that goodness has such a fever that only its death can cure it. Only novelty is wanted, and it is as dangerous to stick to any one way of life for long as it is virtuous to be constant in anything you undertake. There is hardly enough honesty alive to make people safe in their dealings, but there are plenty of guarantees to make partnerships a curse. The wisdom of the world mostly turns on this riddle. This news is old, and yet it is every day's news. Tell me, sir, what kind of man was the Duke?
One that, above all other strifes, contended especially to know / himself.
One who struggled above all else to know himself.
What pleasure was he given to?

Rather rejoicing to see another merry, than merry at anything which / professed to make him rejoice. A gentleman of all temperance. But leave / we him to his events, with a prayer they may prove prosperous, and let / me desire to know how you find Claudio prepared. I am made to / understand that you have lent him visitation.

He was happier seeing others merry than being merry at anything meant to entertain him. A gentleman of complete self-control. But let us leave him to his fortunes, with a prayer that they turn out well, and let me ask how you find Claudio prepared. I understand you have visited him.

He professes to have received no sinister measure from his judge, but / most willingly humbles himself to the determination of justice. Yet had / he framed to himself, by the instruction of his frailty, many deceiving / promises of life, which I, by my good leisure, have discredited to him, / and now he is resolved to die.

He says his judge has not treated him unfairly, and he submits most willingly to the decision of justice. But, led on by his weakness, he had invented many false hopes of life for himself, which I have patiently shown him to be false, and now he is resolved to die.

You have paid the heavens your function, and the prisoner the very debt / of your calling. I have laboured for the poor gentleman to the / extremest shore of my modesty, but my brother justice have I found so / severe that he hath forced me to tell him he is indeed Justice.

You have done your duty to heaven and paid the prisoner what your calling owes him. I have worked for the poor gentleman to the furthest limit of what my position allows, but I have found my colleague so severe in his justice that he has made me tell him he is Justice itself.
If his own life answer the straitness of his proceeding, it shall / become him well; wherein if he chance to fail, he hath sentenced / himself.
If his own life lives up to the strictness of his actions, that will be to his credit; but if he happens to fail, he has sentenced himself.
I am going to visit the prisoner. Fare you well.
I am going to visit the prisoner. Goodbye.

He who the sword of heaven will bear / Should be as holy as severe, / Pattern in himself to know, / Grace to stand, and virtue go; / More nor less to others paying / Than by self-offences weighing. / Shame to him whose cruel striking / Kills for faults of his own liking! / Twice treble shame on Angelo, / To weed my vice, and let his grow! / O, what may man within him hide, / Though angel on the outward side! / How may likeness, made in crimes, / Make practice on the times, / To draw with idle spiders' strings / Most ponderous and substantial things! / Craft against vice I must apply. / With Angelo tonight shall lie / His old betrothed but despised. / So disguise shall, by th' disguised, / Pay with falsehood false exacting, / And perform an old contracting.

The man who carries heaven's sword of justice should be as holy as he is severe. He should find the pattern in himself, with grace to stand firm and virtue to act, punishing others no more and no less than he would weigh his own offences. Shame on the man whose cruel blows kill others for faults he likes to commit himself! Twice and three times shame on Angelo, who weeds out my vice and lets his own grow! Oh, what a man may hide inside, though he looks like an angel on the outside! How false appearances, made up of crimes, can deceive the world, pulling in heavy, solid things with flimsy spiders' threads! I must use cunning against vice. Tonight his old fiancée, whom he scorned, will lie with Angelo. So disguise will use a disguised woman to pay back his false demand with falsehood, and fulfil an old contract.

Take, O take those lips away, / That so sweetly were forsworn, / And those eyes, the break of day, / Lights that do mislead the morn. / But my kisses bring again, / Bring again; / Seals of love, but sealed in vain, / Sealed in vain.

~Take your lips away, oh take them, those lips that broke their promises so sweetly; and take those eyes, bright as daybreak, lights that fool the morning. But bring my kisses back, bring them back: seals of love, but sealed for nothing, sealed for nothing.
Break off thy song, and haste thee quick away; / Here comes a man of comfort, whose advice / Hath often stilled my brawling discontent.
Stop your song and hurry away. Here comes a man of comfort, whose advice has often calmed my noisy unhappiness.
I cry you mercy, sir, and well could wish / You had not found me here so musical. / Let me excuse me, and believe me so, / My mirth it much displeased, but pleased my woe.
I beg your pardon, sir, and I wish you had not found me here enjoying music. Let me explain, and believe me: it did not please my mirth, but it soothed my sorrow.

'Tis good; though music oft hath such a charm / To make bad good and good provoke to harm. / I pray you tell me, hath anybody inquired for me here today? Much upon / this time have I promised here to meet.
That is good, though music often has the power to make bad seem good and stir good to harm. Please tell me, has anyone asked for me here today? I promised to meet someone here at about this time.
You have not been inquired after. I have sat here all day.
No one has asked for you. I have been sitting here all day.
I do constantly believe you. The time is come even now. I shall crave / your forbearance a little. Maybe I will call upon you anon for some / advantage to yourself.
I believe you completely. The moment has come. I must ask you to leave us for a little. I may call you back soon for something to your advantage.
I am always bound to you.
I am always in your debt.
Very well met, and welcome. / What is the news from this good deputy?
Good to see you, and welcome. What is the news from this good deputy?

He hath a garden circummured with brick, / Whose western side is with a vineyard backed; / And to that vineyard is a planched gate / That makes his opening with this bigger key. / This other doth command a little door / Which from the vineyard to the garden leads; / There have I made my promise, upon the / Heavy middle of the night to call on him.

He has a garden walled in with brick, with a vineyard on its western side. The vineyard has a gate of planks that this bigger key opens. This other key unlocks a little door that leads from the vineyard into the garden. That is where I have promised to come to him in the dead middle of the night.
But shall you on your knowledge find this way?
But will you be able to find the way by yourself?
I have ta'en a due and wary note upon't; / With whispering and most guilty diligence, / In action all of precept, he did show me / The way twice o'er.
I took careful note of it. Whispering, and with very guilty care, he showed me the way twice over, with gestures as well as words.
Are there no other tokens / Between you 'greed concerning her observance?
Were there no other signs agreed between you that she must observe?

No, none, but only a repair i' th' dark, / And that I have possessed him my most stay / Can be but brief, for I have made him know / I have a servant comes with me along, / That stays upon me; whose persuasion is / I come about my brother.

No, none, except that I come in the dark; and I have told him I can only stay a short time, because I have made him believe I bring a servant with me who waits for me and thinks I have come about my brother.
'Tis well borne up. / I have not yet made known to Mariana / A word of this.—What ho, within! Come forth.
That is well managed. I have not told Mariana a word of this yet. Hello in there! Come out.
I pray you be acquainted with this maid; / She comes to do you good.
Please get to know this young woman. She has come to do you good.
That is what I want too.
Do you persuade yourself that I respect you?
Are you convinced that I care for you?
Good friar, I know you do, and have found it.
Good friar, I know you do, and I have found it so.
Take, then, this your companion by the hand, / Who hath a story ready for your ear. / I shall attend your leisure; but make haste. / The vaporous night approaches.
Then take your companion by the hand; she has a story ready for you. I will wait for you, but hurry. The misty night is coming.
Will you walk aside with me?

O place and greatness, millions of false eyes / Are stuck upon thee; volumes of report / Run with these false, and most contrarious quest / Upon thy doings; thousand escapes of wit / Make thee the father of their idle dream / And rack thee in their fancies.

Oh rank and greatness, millions of false eyes are fixed on you! Volumes of rumour run after your actions on false and contradictory trails. A thousand flights of wit make you the father of their silly dreams and stretch you on the rack of their imaginations.
She'll take the enterprise upon her, father, / If you advise it.
She'll take on the task, father, if you advise it.
It is not my consent, / But my entreaty too.
I don't just consent to it; I beg her to.
Little have you to say / When you depart from him, but, soft and low, / "Remember now my brother."
You have little to say when you leave him, except, softly and quietly, "Now remember my brother."

Nor, gentle daughter, fear you not at all. / He is your husband on a pre-contract. / To bring you thus together 'tis no sin, / Sith that the justice of your title to him / Doth flourish the deceit. Come, let us go; / Our corn's to reap, for yet our tithe's to sow.

And, gentle daughter, don't you be afraid at all. He is your husband by an earlier contract. It is no sin to bring you together like this, since the justice of your claim on him makes the trick an honest one. Come, let's go. We have corn to reap, because we still have the seed to sow.
Come hither, sirrah. Can you cut off a man's head?
Come here, fellow. Can you cut off a man's head?
If the man be a bachelor, sir, I can; but if he be a married man, he's / his wife's head, and I can never cut off a woman's head.
If the man's a bachelor, sir, I can; but if he's married, he's his wife's head, and I could never cut off a woman's head.

Come, sir, leave me your snatches, and yield me a direct answer. / Tomorrow morning are to die Claudio and Barnardine. Here is in our / prison a common executioner, who in his office lacks a helper; if you / will take it on you to assist him, it shall redeem you from your gyves; / if not, you shall have your full time of imprisonment, and your / deliverance with an unpitied whipping; for you have been a notorious / bawd.

Come on, sir, spare me your quips and give me a straight answer. Tomorrow morning Claudio and Barnardine are to die. We have a common executioner here in the prison who needs an assistant. If you'll agree to help him, it will free you from your chains. If not, you'll serve your full sentence and be let out with a whipping nobody will pity, because you have been a notorious pimp.
Sir, I have been an unlawful bawd time out of mind, but yet I will be / content to be a lawful hangman. I would be glad to receive some / instruction from my fellow-partner.
Sir, I've been an unlawful pimp for as long as anyone can remember, but I'll be happy to be a lawful hangman. I'd be glad to have some lessons from my new partner.
What ho, Abhorson! Where's Abhorson, there?

Sirrah, here's a fellow will help you tomorrow in your execution. If / you think it meet, compound with him by the year, and let him abide / here with you; if not, use him for the present, and dismiss him. He / cannot plead his estimation with you; he hath been a bawd.

Fellow, here's a man who will help you tomorrow with your execution. If you think fit, hire him by the year and let him live here with you; if not, use him for now and then let him go. He can't stand on his dignity with you; he has been a pimp.
A bawd, sir? Fie upon him, he will discredit our mystery.
A pimp, sir? Shame on him! He'll disgrace our craft.
Go to, sir; you weigh equally. A feather will turn the scale.
Come off it, sir; you two weigh the same. A feather would tip the scales.
Pray, sir, by your good favour—for surely, sir, a good favour you have, / but that you have a hanging look—do you call, sir, your occupation a / mystery?
Excuse me, sir, if you please, for you surely have a good face, sir, except that it has a hanging look: do you call your occupation a craft, sir?

Painting, sir, I have heard say, is a mystery; and your whores, sir, / being members of my occupation, using painting, do prove my occupation / a mystery. But what mystery there should be in hanging, if I should be / hanged, I cannot imagine.

Painting, sir, I've heard, is a craft; and your whores, sir, who are members of my profession, use paint, which proves my profession is a craft. But what craft there could be in hanging, if I were to be hanged, I can't imagine.

Every true man's apparel fits your thief. If it be too little for your / thief, your true man thinks it big enough; if it be too big for your / thief, your thief thinks it little enough. So every true man's apparel / fits your thief.

Every honest man's clothes fit a thief. If they're too small for the thief, the honest man thinks they're big enough; if they're too big for the thief, the thief thinks they're small enough. So every honest man's clothes fit a thief. (The hangman keeps his victims' clothes.)
Sir, I will serve him; for I do find your hangman is a more penitent / trade than your bawd. He doth oftener ask forgiveness.
Sir, I'll work for him, because I find a hangman is a more repentant trade than a pimp: he asks for forgiveness more often.
You, sirrah, provide your block and your axe tomorrow four o'clock.
You, fellow, have your block and your axe ready tomorrow at four o'clock.
Come on, bawd. I will instruct thee in my trade. Follow.
Come on, pimp. I'll teach you my trade. Follow me.
I do desire to learn, sir; and I hope, if you have occasion to use me / for your own turn, you shall find me yare. For truly, sir, for your / kindness I owe you a good turn.
I'm keen to learn, sir; and I hope, if you ever need me to do the job on you yourself, you'll find me quick. Honestly, sir, for your kindness I owe you a good turn.
Th' one has my pity; not a jot the other, / Being a murderer, though he were my brother.
One of them has my pity; the other not a scrap, because he is a murderer, even if he were my brother.
Look, here's the warrant, Claudio, for thy death. / 'Tis now dead midnight, and by eight tomorrow / Thou must be made immortal. Where's Barnardine?
Look, Claudio, here's the warrant for your death. It is now the middle of the night, and by eight tomorrow you must be made immortal. Where's Barnardine?
As fast locked up in sleep as guiltless labour / When it lies starkly in the traveller's bones. / He will not wake.
As soundly locked in sleep as honest tiredness when it lies stiff in a traveller's bones. He won't wake up.
Who can do good on him? / Well, go, prepare yourself. [Knocking within] But hark, what noise? / Heaven give your spirits comfort!
Who can do him any good? Well, go and prepare yourself. (Knocking) But listen, what's that noise? Heaven comfort your spirit!
By and by!— / I hope it is some pardon or reprieve / For the most gentle Claudio.
Just a moment! I hope it is some pardon or reprieve for the most gentle Claudio.
The best and wholesom'st spirits of the night / Envelop you, good Provost! Who called here of late?
May the best and most healing spirits of the night surround you, good Provost! Who has called here recently?
No one since the curfew bell.
They will then, ere't be long.
Then they will come before long.
What comfort is there for Claudio?

Not so, not so. His life is paralleled / Even with the stroke and line of his great justice. / He doth with holy abstinence subdue / That in himself which he spurs on his power / To qualify in others. Were he mealed with that / Which he corrects, then were he tyrannous; / But this being so, he's just.

Not so, not so. His life runs exactly parallel with the stroke and line of his great justice. With holy self-denial he masters in himself the very things he uses his power to curb in others. If he were stained with what he punishes, he would be a tyrant; but since he is not, he is just.
Now are they come. / This is a gentle provost. Seldom when / The steeled gaoler is the friend of men.
Now they have come. This is a kind provost. It is rare for a hard-hearted jailer to be a friend to men.
How now? What noise? That spirit's possessed with haste / That wounds th' unsisting postern with these strokes.
What's this? What's that noise? Whoever is beating the unresisting back gate like that must be in a great hurry.
There he must stay until the officer / Arise to let him in. He is called up.
He will have to wait there until the officer gets up to let him in. He has been called.
Have you no countermand for Claudio yet, / But he must die tomorrow?
Have you still no order cancelling Claudio's death? Must he die tomorrow?
As near the dawning, Provost, as it is, / You shall hear more ere morning.
Close as it is to dawn, Provost, you will hear more before morning.

Happily / You something know, yet I believe there comes / No countermand. No such example have we. / Besides, upon the very siege of justice / Lord Angelo hath to the public ear / Professed the contrary.
Perhaps you know something, but I don't believe any countermand will come. There has never been such a case. Besides, Lord Angelo has publicly declared the opposite from the very seat of justice.

My lord hath sent you this note, and by me this further charge: that / you swerve not from the smallest article of it, neither in time, / matter, or other circumstance. Good morrow; for, as I take it, it is / almost day.

My lord has sent you this note, and through me this further order: that you do not depart from the smallest detail of it, in time, matter or any other circumstance. Good morning, for I believe it is almost day.

[Aside] This is his pardon, purchased by such sin / For which the pardoner himself is in. / Hence hath offence his quick celerity, / When it is borne in high authority. / When vice makes mercy, mercy's so extended / That for the fault's love is th' offender friended. / Now, sir, what news?

(Aside) This is his pardon, bought with the very sin the pardoner himself is guilty of. That is why crime moves so fast when it is carried out by those in high authority. When vice grants mercy, mercy goes so far that the offender is befriended for love of his fault. Now, sir, what's the news?
I told you: Lord Angelo, belike thinking me remiss in mine office, / awakens me with this unwonted putting-on; methinks strangely, for he / hath not used it before.
As I told you: Lord Angelo, probably thinking I'm careless in my duty, stirs me up with this unusual urging. It's strange, I think, because he has never done it before.

[Reads] Whatsoever you may hear to the contrary, let Claudio be / executed by four of the clock, and in the afternoon, Barnardine. For my / better satisfaction, let me have Claudio's head sent me by five. Let / this be duly performed, with a thought that more depends on it than we / must yet deliver. Thus fail not to do your office, as you will answer / it at your peril. / What say you to this, sir?

(Reads) "Whatever you may hear to the contrary, have Claudio executed by four o'clock, and Barnardine in the afternoon. For my greater satisfaction, have Claudio's head sent to me by five. See that this is carried out properly, remembering that more depends on it than we can yet reveal. Do not fail in your duty, or you will answer for it at your peril." What do you say to this, sir?
What is that Barnardine who is to be executed in th' afternoon?
Who is this Barnardine who is to be executed in the afternoon?
A Bohemian born, but here nursed up and bred; one that is a prisoner / nine years old.
A Bohemian by birth, but brought up and raised here. He has been a prisoner for nine years.
How came it that the absent Duke had not either delivered him to his / liberty, or executed him? I have heard it was ever his manner to do so.
How is it that the absent Duke never either set him free or had him executed? I have heard that was always his way.
His friends still wrought reprieves for him; and indeed, his fact till / now in the government of Lord Angelo, came not to an undoubtful proof.
His friends kept getting reprieves for him; and in fact his crime was never proved beyond doubt until now, under Lord Angelo's government.
Most manifest, and not denied by himself.
Perfectly clear, and he doesn't deny it himself.
Hath he borne himself penitently in prison? How seems he to be touched?
Has he behaved like a repentant man in prison? How does he seem to be affected?
A man that apprehends death no more dreadfully but as a drunken sleep; / careless, reckless, and fearless of what's past, present, or to come; / insensible of mortality and desperately mortal.

He is a man who fears death no more than a drunken sleep; careless, reckless and fearless of what has been, what is and what is to come; with no sense of his mortality, and in desperate danger of dying.

He will hear none. He hath evermore had the liberty of the prison; give / him leave to escape hence, he would not. Drunk many times a day, if not / many days entirely drunk. We have very oft awaked him, as if to carry / him to execution, and showed him a seeming warrant for it. It hath not / moved him at all.

He won't listen to any. He has always had the run of the prison; if you gave him the chance to escape, he wouldn't take it. He's drunk many times a day, if not completely drunk for days at a time. We have very often woken him as if to take him to execution, and shown him a fake warrant for it. It hasn't moved him at all.

More of him anon. There is written in your brow, Provost, honesty and / constancy; if I read it not truly, my ancient skill beguiles me. But in / the boldness of my cunning I will lay myself in hazard. Claudio, whom / here you have warrant to execute, is no greater forfeit to the law than / Angelo who hath sentenced him. To make you understand this in a / manifested effect, I crave but four days' respite, for the which you / are to do me both a present and a dangerous courtesy.

More about him later. Honesty and steadiness are written on your forehead, Provost; if I don't read it right, my long experience has fooled me. But, trusting boldly in my judgment, I will take a risk. Claudio, whom you have a warrant to execute here, has broken the law no more than Angelo who sentenced him. To make you see this proved in fact, I ask only for four days' delay, for which you must do me a favour, both immediate and dangerous.
Alack, how may I do it? Having the hour limited, and an express / command, under penalty, to deliver his head in the view of Angelo? I / may make my case as Claudio's, to cross this in the smallest.

Oh, how can I do that, when the hour is fixed and I have an express order, under penalty, to deliver his head to Angelo for him to see? If I go against this in the smallest way, I may end up like Claudio.
By the vow of mine order, I warrant you, if my instructions may be your / guide. Let this Barnardine be this morning executed, and his head borne / to Angelo.
By the vow of my order, I guarantee you will be safe if you follow my instructions. Have this Barnardine executed this morning, and take his head to Angelo.
Angelo hath seen them both, and will discover the favour.
Angelo has seen them both and will recognise the face.

O, death's a great disguiser, and you may add to it. Shave the head and / tie the beard, and say it was the desire of the penitent to be so bared / before his death. You know the course is common. If anything fall to / you upon this, more than thanks and good fortune, by the saint whom I / profess, I will plead against it with my life.

Oh, death is a great disguiser, and you can add to it. Shave the head and tie up the beard, and say it was the prisoner's wish, in his repentance, to be shaved like that before he died. You know it's commonly done. If anything comes to you from this but thanks and good fortune, I swear by the saint I serve that I will defend you with my life.
Pardon me, good father; it is against my oath.
Forgive me, good father, it is against my oath.
Were you sworn to the Duke, or to the Deputy?
Did you swear to serve the Duke, or the deputy?
To him and to his substitutes.
The Duke and those who stand in for him.
You will think you have made no offence if the Duke avouch the justice / of your dealing?
Will you think you have done no wrong if the Duke vouches that you acted justly?
But what likelihood is in that?

Not a resemblance, but a certainty. Yet since I see you fearful, that / neither my coat, integrity, nor persuasion, can with ease attempt you, / I will go further than I meant, to pluck all fears out of you. Look / you, sir, here is the hand and seal of the Duke. You know the / character, I doubt not, and the signet is not strange to you.

Not likely: certain. But since I see you are afraid, and neither my habit, my honesty nor my persuasion can easily move you, I will go further than I intended to take all your fears away. Look, sir, here is the Duke's handwriting and seal. You know his hand, I'm sure, and the seal is familiar to you.

The contents of this is the return of the Duke; you shall anon / over-read it at your pleasure, where you shall find within these two / days he will be here. This is a thing that Angelo knows not; for he / this very day receives letters of strange tenour, perchance of the / Duke's death, perchance entering into some monastery; but, by chance, / nothing of what is writ. Look, th' unfolding star calls up the / shepherd. Put not yourself into amazement how these things should be. / All difficulties are but easy when they are known. Call your / executioner, and off with Barnardine's head. I will give him a present / shrift, and advise him for a better place. Yet you are amazed; but this / shall absolutely resolve you. Come away; it is almost clear dawn.

This letter announces the return of the Duke. You can read it through at your leisure in a moment, and you will find he will be here within two days. Angelo does not know this, because today he is receiving letters with strange news, perhaps of the Duke's death, perhaps of his entering a monastery, but none of it what is written here. Look, the morning star is calling the shepherd to unfold his sheep. Don't be bewildered about how all this can be. Every difficulty is easy once it is understood. Call your executioner, and off with Barnardine's head. I will hear his confession at once and advise him for a better place. You are still amazed, but this will settle your mind completely. Come; it's almost broad daylight.

I am as well acquainted here as I was in our house of profession. One / would think it were Mistress Overdone's own house, for here be many of / her old customers. First, here's young Master Rash; he's in for a / commodity of brown paper and old ginger, nine score and seventeen / pounds; of which he made five marks ready money. Marry, then ginger was / not much in request, for the old women were all dead. Then is there / here one Master Caper, at the suit of Master Three-pile the mercer, for / some four suits of peach-coloured satin, which now peaches him a / beggar. Then have we here young Dizie, and young Master Deep-vow, and / Master Copperspur, and Master Starve-lackey, the rapier and dagger man, / and young Drop-heir that killed lusty Pudding, and Master Forthright / the tilter, and brave Master Shoe-tie the great traveller, and wild / Half-can that stabbed Pots, and I think forty more, all great doers in / our trade, and are now "for the Lord's sake."

I feel as much at home here as I did in our house of business. You'd think it was Mistress Overdone's own place, there are so many of her old customers here. First, there's young Master Rash. He's in for a loan of brown paper and old ginger worth a hundred and ninety-seven pounds, which he sold for five marks cash. Well, ginger wasn't much in demand then, because all the old women had died. Then there's a Master Caper, sued by Master Three-pile the cloth dealer for four suits of peach-coloured satin, which has now impeached him as a beggar. Then we have young Dizzy, young Master Deep-vow, Master Copperspur, Master Starve-lackey the rapier-and-dagger man, young Drop-heir who killed lusty Pudding, Master Forthright the jouster, brave Master Shoe-tie the great traveller, wild Half-can who stabbed Pots, and I think forty more, all big dealers in our trade, and all now begging through the bars "for the Lord's sake".
Master Barnardine! You must rise and be hanged, Master Barnardine.
Master Barnardine! You must get up and be hanged, Master Barnardine.
[Within] A pox o' your throats! Who makes that noise there? What are / you?
(From inside) Damn your throats! Who's making that noise? Who are you?
Your friends, sir; the hangman. You must be so good, sir, to rise and / be put to death.
Your friends, sir: the hangman. Be so good, sir, as to get up and be put to death.
[Within] Away, you rogue, away; I am sleepy.
(From inside) Go away, you rogue, go away. I'm sleepy.
Tell him he must awake, and that quickly too.
Tell him he must wake up, and quickly too.
