Pray, Master Barnardine, awake till you are executed, and sleep / afterwards.
Please, Master Barnardine, stay awake until you're executed, and sleep afterwards.
Go in to him, and fetch him out.
Go in and fetch him out.
He is coming, sir, he is coming. I hear his straw rustle.
He's coming, sir, he's coming. I can hear his straw rustling.
Is the axe upon the block, sirrah?
Is the axe on the block, fellow?
How now, Abhorson? What's the news with you?
Well, Abhorson? What news do you have?
Truly, sir, I would desire you to clap into your prayers; for, look / you, the warrant's come.
Honestly, sir, I'd like you to get on with your prayers, because, look, the warrant has come.
You rogue, I have been drinking all night; I am not fitted for't.
You rogue, I've been drinking all night. I'm not fit for it.
O, the better, sir; for he that drinks all night and is hanged betimes / in the morning may sleep the sounder all the next day.
Oh, all the better, sir, because a man who drinks all night and is hanged early in the morning will sleep all the sounder all the next day.
Look you, sir, here comes your ghostly father. Do we jest now, think / you?
Look, sir, here comes your spiritual father. Do you think we're joking now?
Sir, induced by my charity, and hearing how hastily you are to depart, / I am come to advise you, comfort you, and pray with you.
Sir, moved by charity, and hearing how soon you are to depart, I have come to advise you, comfort you and pray with you.
Friar, not I. I have been drinking hard all night, and I will have more / time to prepare me, or they shall beat out my brains with billets. I / will not consent to die this day, that's certain.
Not me, friar. I've been drinking hard all night, and I'll have more time to get ready, or they'll have to beat my brains out with logs. I won't agree to die today, that's for sure.
O, sir, you must; and therefore I beseech you / Look forward on the journey you shall go.
Oh, sir, you must; and so I beg you, look ahead to the journey you are about to take.
I swear I will not die today for any man's persuasion.
I swear I won't die today, whoever tries to persuade me.
Not a word. If you have anything to say to me, come to my ward, for / thence will not I today.
Not a word. If you've got anything to say to me, come to my cell, because I'm not leaving it today.
Unfit to live or die. O gravel heart! / After him, fellows; bring him to the block.
Unfit to live or die. Oh, heart of gravel! Go after him, fellows, and bring him to the block.
Now, sir, how do you find the prisoner?
Now, sir, how do you find the prisoner?
A creature unprepared, unmeet for death; / And to transport him in the mind he is / Were damnable.
A creature unprepared and unfit for death; and to send him off in his present state of mind would be damnable.

Here in the prison, father, / There died this morning of a cruel fever / One Ragozine, a most notorious pirate, / A man of Claudio's years; his beard and head / Just of his colour. What if we do omit / This reprobate till he were well inclined, / And satisfy the Deputy with the visage / Of Ragozine, more like to Claudio?

Here in the prison, father, a man called Ragozine died this morning of a cruel fever. He was a notorious pirate, a man of Claudio's age, with beard and hair exactly his colour. What if we leave this wretch until he is in a better frame of mind, and satisfy the deputy with Ragozine's face, which is more like Claudio's?

O, 'tis an accident that heaven provides! / Dispatch it presently; the hour draws on / Prefixed by Angelo. See this be done, / And sent according to command, whiles I / Persuade this rude wretch willingly to die.
Oh, this is a chance sent by heaven! Do it at once. The hour Angelo set is coming. See that it is done and the head sent as ordered, while I persuade this rough wretch to die willingly.
This shall be done, good father, presently. / But Barnardine must die this afternoon; / And how shall we continue Claudio, / To save me from the danger that might come / If he were known alive?
It shall be done at once, good father. But Barnardine must die this afternoon. And how shall we keep Claudio, to save me from the danger I could be in if he were known to be alive?
Let this be done: / Put them in secret holds, both Barnardine and Claudio. / Ere twice the sun hath made his journal greeting / To yonder generation, you shall find / Your safety manifested.
Do this: put them both, Barnardine and Claudio, in secret cells. Before the sun has twice made its daily greeting to the people beyond us, you will find your safety made clear.
I am entirely at your service.
Quick, dispatch, and send the head to Angelo.
Quick, hurry, and send the head to Angelo.

Now will I write letters to Angelo, / The Provost, he shall bear them, whose contents / Shall witness to him I am near at home; / And that by great injunctions I am bound / To enter publicly. Him I'll desire / To meet me at the consecrated fount, / A league below the city; and from thence, / By cold gradation and well-balanced form. / We shall proceed with Angelo.

Now I will write letters to Angelo, and the Provost shall carry them, saying that I am near home and that, for important reasons, I must make a public entry. I will ask him to meet me at the holy spring, three miles outside the city; and from there, by careful steps and in proper order, we shall proceed against Angelo.
Here is the head; I'll carry it myself.
Here is the head. I'll take it myself.
Convenient is it. Make a swift return; / For I would commune with you of such things / That want no ear but yours.
That is best. Come back quickly, because I want to talk to you about things that no one else should hear.
I'll be as fast as I can.

The tongue of Isabel. She's come to know / If yet her brother's pardon be come hither. / But I will keep her ignorant of her good, / To make her heavenly comforts of despair / When it is least expected.

That is Isabel's voice. She has come to find out whether her brother's pardon has arrived. But I will keep her in ignorance of her good fortune, so as to turn her despair into heavenly comfort when she least expects it.
Good morning to you, fair and gracious daughter.
Good morning to you, lovely and gracious daughter.
The better, given me by so holy a man. / Hath yet the Deputy sent my brother's pardon?
It is a better morning for being wished by so holy a man. Has the deputy sent my brother's pardon yet?
He hath released him, Isabel, from the world. / His head is off, and sent to Angelo.
He has released him from the world, Isabel. His head has been cut off and sent to Angelo.
Nay, but it is not so.
It is no other. / Show your wisdom, daughter, in your close patience.
It is just so. Show your wisdom, daughter, by keeping patiently quiet.
O, I will to him and pluck out his eyes!
Oh, I'll go to him and tear his eyes out!
You shall not be admitted to his sight.
You won't be allowed to see him.
Unhappy Claudio! Wretched Isabel! / Injurious world! Most damned Angelo!
Unhappy Claudio! Wretched Isabel! Cruel world! Utterly damned Angelo!

This nor hurts him nor profits you a jot. / Forbear it, therefore; give your cause to heaven. / Mark what I say, which you shall find / By every syllable a faithful verity. / The Duke comes home tomorrow;—nay, dry your eyes. / One of our convent, and his confessor, / Gives me this instance. Already he hath carried / Notice to Escalus and Angelo, / Who do prepare to meet him at the gates, / There to give up their power. If you can, pace your wisdom / In that good path that I would wish it go, / And you shall have your bosom on this wretch, / Grace of the Duke, revenges to your heart, / And general honour.

This doesn't hurt him or help you in the least. So stop it, and leave your cause to heaven. Listen to what I say; you will find every syllable of it is the plain truth. The Duke comes home tomorrow. No, dry your eyes. A brother of our convent, his confessor, tells me so. He has already taken the news to Escalus and Angelo, who are getting ready to meet him at the gates and hand back their power there. If you can, walk your wisdom down the good path I want it to take, and you will have your heart's desire on this wretch, the Duke's favour, revenge to satisfy you, and honour from everyone.
I will do as you direct.

This letter, then, to Friar Peter give; / 'Tis that he sent me of the Duke's return. / Say, by this token, I desire his company / At Mariana's house tonight. Her cause and yours / I'll perfect him withal, and he shall bring you / Before the Duke; and to the head of Angelo / Accuse him home and home. For my poor self, / I am combined by a sacred vow, / And shall be absent. Wend you with this letter. / Command these fretting waters from your eyes / With a light heart; trust not my holy order, / If I pervert your course.—Who's here?

Then give this letter to Friar Peter. It is the one he sent me about the Duke's return. Tell him that, by this sign, I want him to come to Mariana's house tonight. I will tell him everything about her case and yours, and he will bring you before the Duke, and you can accuse Angelo to his face, all the way. As for poor me, I am bound by a sacred vow and must be absent. Go with this letter. Command those stinging tears to stop, and keep your heart light. Don't trust my holy order if I lead you wrong. Who's here?
Good even. Friar, where is the Provost?
Good evening. Friar, where is the Provost?

O pretty Isabella, I am pale at mine heart to see thine eyes so red. / Thou must be patient. I am fain to dine and sup with water and bran. I / dare not for my head fill my belly. One fruitful meal would set me / to't. But they say the Duke will be here tomorrow. By my troth, Isabel, / I loved thy brother. If the old fantastical duke of dark corners had / been at home, he had lived.

Oh, pretty Isabella, my heart goes pale to see your eyes so red. You must be patient. I have to make do with bread and water for dinner and supper; I daren't fill my belly for fear of losing my head. One good meal would set me off. But they say the Duke will be here tomorrow. Honestly, Isabel, I loved your brother. If the strange old Duke who lurks in dark corners had been at home, your brother would have lived.
Sir, the Duke is marvellous little beholding to your reports; but the / best is, he lives not in them.
Sir, the Duke owes very little thanks to your reports of him; but the good thing is that his real life is not in them.
Friar, thou knowest not the Duke so well as I do. He's a better woodman / than thou tak'st him for.
Friar, you don't know the Duke as well as I do. He's a better hunter of women than you think.
Well, you'll answer this one day. Fare ye well.
Well, you'll answer for this one day. Goodbye.
Nay, tarry, I'll go along with thee. I can tell thee pretty tales of / the Duke.
No, wait, I'll come with you. I can tell you some fine stories about the Duke.
You have told me too many of him already, sir, if they be true; if not / true, none were enough.
You have told me too many already, sir, if they are true; and if they're not, even one was too many.
I was once before him for getting a wench with child.
I was once brought before him for getting a girl pregnant.
Yes, marry, did I; but I was fain to forswear it. They would else have / married me to the rotten medlar.
Yes, by heaven, I did; but I had to swear I hadn't. Otherwise they would have married me to that rotten fruit.
Sir, your company is fairer than honest. Rest you well.
Sir, your company is more pleasant than honest. Goodbye.
By my troth, I'll go with thee to the lane's end. If bawdy talk offend / you, we'll have very little of it. Nay, friar, I am a kind of burr; I / shall stick.
Honestly, I'll go with you to the end of the lane. If dirty talk offends you, we'll keep it to a minimum. No, friar, I'm a kind of burr: I'll stick.
Every letter he hath writ hath disvouched other.
Every letter he has written has contradicted the one before.
In most uneven and distracted manner. His actions show much like to / madness; pray heaven his wisdom be not tainted. And why meet him at the / gates and redeliver our authorities there?
In a most erratic, confused way. His actions look very like madness; heaven grant his mind is not affected. And why meet him at the gates and hand our authority back there?
And why should we proclaim it in an hour before his entering, that if / any crave redress of injustice, they should exhibit their petitions in / the street?
And why should we announce, an hour before he enters, that anyone who wants an injustice put right should present their petitions in the street?
He shows his reason for that: to have a dispatch of complaints, and to / deliver us from devices hereafter, which shall then have no power to / stand against us.
He gives his reason for that: to have all complaints dealt with at once, and to protect us from plots later on, which will then have no power against us.
Well, I beseech you, let it be proclaimed. / Betimes i' th' morn I'll call you at your house. / Give notice to such men of sort and suit / As are to meet him.
Well, please have it announced. I will call for you at your house early in the morning. Let the men of rank and standing who are to meet him know.
I shall, sir. Fare you well.

Good night. / This deed unshapes me quite, makes me unpregnant / And dull to all proceedings. A deflowered maid; / And by an eminent body that enforced / The law against it! But that her tender shame / Will not proclaim against her maiden loss, / How might she tongue me! Yet reason dares her no, / For my authority bears so credent bulk / That no particular scandal once can touch / But it confounds the breather. He should have lived, / Save that his riotous youth, with dangerous sense, / Might in the times to come have ta'en revenge / By so receiving a dishonoured life / With ransom of such shame. Would yet he had lived. / Alack, when once our grace we have forgot, / Nothing goes right; we would, and we would not.

Good night. This deed has unmade me completely. It leaves me witless and dull for any business. A young woman deflowered, and by a man of high position who enforced the law against that very thing! If her modest shame did not keep her from announcing the loss of her virginity, how she could denounce me! But reason tells her not to, because my authority carries such solid credit that no private accusation can touch it without ruining the person who makes it. He should have lived, except that his wild young blood, feeling the dishonour, might have taken revenge in time to come for being given a disgraced life bought with such shame. And yet I wish he had lived. Oh, once we have forgotten grace, nothing goes right. We want to, and we don't want to.

These letters at fit time deliver me. / The Provost knows our purpose and our plot. / The matter being afoot, keep your instruction / And hold you ever to our special drift, / Though sometimes you do blench from this to that / As cause doth minister. Go call at Flavius' house, / And tell him where I stay. Give the like notice / To Valencius, Rowland, and to Crassus, / And bid them bring the trumpets to the gate. / But send me Flavius first.

Deliver these letters for me at the right time. The Provost knows our purpose and our plan. Now that it is under way, keep to your instructions and always hold to our particular aim, even if you sometimes have to swerve from one thing to another as the occasion demands. Go and call at Flavius's house and tell him where I am. Give the same message to Valencius, Rowland and Crassus, and tell them to bring the trumpeters to the gate. But send Flavius to me first.
I thank thee, Varrius, thou hast made good haste. / Come, we will walk. There's other of our friends / Will greet us here anon. My gentle Varrius.
Thank you, Varrius, you have come very quickly. Come, let us walk. Others of our friends will greet us here soon. My gentle Varrius.
To speak so indirectly I am loath; / I would say the truth, but to accuse him so / That is your part; yet I am advised to do it, / He says, to veil full purpose.
I hate to speak in such a roundabout way. I would rather tell the truth, but accusing him like that is your part. Still, he advises me to do it, he says, to hide our full purpose.
Besides, he tells me that, if peradventure / He speak against me on the adverse side, / I should not think it strange, for 'tis a physic / That's bitter to sweet end.
Besides, he tells me that if he happens to speak against me, on the other side, I shouldn't think it strange, because it is bitter medicine for a sweet result.
O, peace, the friar is come.
Oh, hush, the friar has come.

Come, I have found you out a stand most fit, / Where you may have such vantage on the Duke / He shall not pass you. Twice have the trumpets sounded. / The generous and gravest citizens / Have hent the gates, and very near upon / The Duke is entering. Therefore hence, away.

Come, I have found you a perfect place to stand, where you will be so well placed for the Duke that he can't pass you by. The trumpets have sounded twice. The noblest and most respected citizens have taken up their places at the gates, and the Duke is about to enter. So come on, let's go.
My very worthy cousin, fairly met. / Our old and faithful friend, we are glad to see you.
My most worthy cousin, well met. Our old and faithful friend, we are glad to see you.
Happy return be to your royal grace!
A happy return to your royal Grace!

Many and hearty thankings to you both. / We have made inquiry of you, and we hear / Such goodness of your justice that our soul / Cannot but yield you forth to public thanks, / Forerunning more requital.
Many warm thanks to you both. We have asked about you, and we hear such good things of your justice that we cannot help thanking you publicly, ahead of greater rewards.
You make my bonds still greater.
You make me even more indebted to you.

O, your desert speaks loud, and I should wrong it / To lock it in the wards of covert bosom, / When it deserves with characters of brass / A forted residence 'gainst the tooth of time / And rasure of oblivion. Give me your hand / And let the subject see, to make them know / That outward courtesies would fain proclaim / Favours that keep within.—Come, Escalus, / You must walk by us on our other hand. / And good supporters are you.

Oh, your merit speaks loudly, and I would wrong it if I locked it away inside my heart, when it deserves to be carved in brass and kept in a fortress against the teeth of time and the erasing of forgetfulness. Give me your hand, and let the people see it, so they know that outward courtesy is eager to show the favour held within. Come, Escalus, you must walk on my other side. You are both good supporters.
Now is your time. Speak loud, and kneel before him.
Now is your chance. Speak loudly, and kneel in front of him.

Justice, O royal Duke! Vail your regard / Upon a wronged—I would fain have said, a maid. / O worthy prince, dishonour not your eye / By throwing it on any other object / Till you have heard me in my true complaint, / And given me justice, justice, justice, justice!

Justice, oh royal Duke! Lower your eyes to a wronged... I wanted to say, maiden. Oh worthy prince, do not dishonour your eyes by turning them on anything else until you have heard my true complaint and given me justice, justice, justice, justice!
Relate your wrongs. In what? By whom? Be brief. / Here is Lord Angelo shall give you justice. / Reveal yourself to him.
Tell us your wrongs. In what? By whom? Be brief. Here is Lord Angelo, who will give you justice. Explain yourself to him.

O worthy Duke, / You bid me seek redemption of the devil. / Hear me yourself, for that which I must speak / Must either punish me, not being believed, / Or wring redress from you. Hear me, O hear me, here!

Oh worthy Duke, you are telling me to ask the devil for salvation. Hear me yourself, because what I have to say must either get me punished, if I am not believed, or force you to put it right. Hear me, oh hear me, here!
My lord, her wits, I fear me, are not firm. / She hath been a suitor to me for her brother, / Cut off by course of justice.
My lord, I am afraid her mind is not steady. She came to me to plead for her brother, who has been executed in the course of justice.
And she will speak most bitterly and strange.
And she will say very bitter and strange things.

Most strange, but yet most truly will I speak. / That Angelo's forsworn, is it not strange? / That Angelo's a murderer, is't not strange? / That Angelo is an adulterous thief, / An hypocrite, a virgin-violator, / Is it not strange and strange?

Very strange, but very true is what I'll say. That Angelo has broken his word, isn't that strange? That Angelo is a murderer, isn't that strange? That Angelo is an adulterous thief, a hypocrite, a violator of virgins, isn't that strange and strange again?
Nay, it is ten times strange.
Why, it is ten times strange.
It is not truer he is Angelo / Than this is all as true as it is strange. / Nay, it is ten times true, for truth is truth / To th' end of reckoning.
It is no truer that he is Angelo than that all this is as true as it is strange. No, it is ten times true, because truth is truth to the end of time.
Away with her. Poor soul, / She speaks this in th' infirmity of sense.
Take her away. Poor soul, she says this because her mind is sick.

O Prince, I conjure thee, as thou believ'st / There is another comfort than this world, / That thou neglect me not with that opinion / That I am touched with madness. Make not impossible / That which but seems unlike. 'Tis not impossible / But one, the wicked'st caitiff on the ground, / May seem as shy, as grave, as just, as absolute, / As Angelo; even so may Angelo, / In all his dressings, characts, titles, forms, / Be an arch-villain. Believe it, royal Prince, / If he be less, he's nothing; but he's more, / Had I more name for badness.

Oh prince, I beg you, as you believe there is a comfort beyond this world, don't dismiss me by thinking I am touched with madness. Don't make something impossible just because it seems unlikely. It is not impossible that the most wicked wretch on earth could seem as modest, as serious, as just and as perfect as Angelo; and in the same way Angelo, in all his robes, badges, titles and outward forms, could be an arch-villain. Believe it, royal prince: if he is any less than that, he is nothing; but he is more, if I had more words for wickedness.
By mine honesty, / If she be mad, as I believe no other, / Her madness hath the oddest frame of sense, / Such a dependency of thing on thing, / As e'er I heard in madness.
On my honour, if she is mad, as I can only believe, her madness has the strangest pattern of sense, with one thing following from another, that I ever heard in madness.
O gracious Duke, / Harp not on that; nor do not banish reason / For inequality; but let your reason serve / To make the truth appear where it seems hid, / And hide the false seems true.

Oh gracious Duke, don't keep harping on that, and don't throw out reason because the two of us are unequal. Use your reason instead to bring out the truth where it seems hidden, and hide the falsehood that seems true.
Many that are not mad / Have, sure, more lack of reason. What would you say?
Many people who are not mad certainly have less reason than this. What do you want to say?

I am the sister of one Claudio, / Condemned upon the act of fornication / To lose his head; condemned by Angelo. / I, in probation of a sisterhood, / Was sent to by my brother; one Lucio / As then the messenger.

I am the sister of a man named Claudio, condemned to lose his head for the act of fornication; condemned by Angelo. I was in my trial period before joining a sisterhood when my brother sent to me. A man named Lucio was the messenger.
That's I, an't like your Grace. / I came to her from Claudio and desired her / To try her gracious fortune with Lord Angelo / For her poor brother's pardon.
That's me, if it please your Grace. I came to her from Claudio and asked her to try her gracious luck with Lord Angelo for her poor brother's pardon.
You were not bid to speak.
You were not asked to speak.
No, my good lord, / Nor wished to hold my peace.
No, my good lord, nor asked to keep quiet.
I wish you now, then; / Pray you take note of it; and when you have / A business for yourself, pray heaven you then / Be perfect.
Then I ask you now. Please take note of it; and when you have business of your own to answer for, pray heaven you are word perfect then.
The warrant's for yourself. Take heed to it.
The guarantee is on your own head. Be careful of it.
This gentleman told somewhat of my tale.
This gentleman has told part of my story.
It may be right, but you are i' the wrong / To speak before your time.—Proceed.
It may be right, but you are wrong to speak out of turn. Go on.
I went / To this pernicious caitiff deputy.
I went to this wicked, villainous deputy.
Pardon it; / The phrase is to the matter.
Forgive it; the words fit the facts.
Corrected again. The facts; go on.

In brief, to set the needless process by: / How I persuaded, how I prayed and kneeled, / How he refelled me, and how I replied— / For this was of much length—the vile conclusion / I now begin with grief and shame to utter. / He would not, but by gift of my chaste body / To his concupiscible intemperate lust, / Release my brother; and after much debatement, / My sisterly remorse confutes mine honour, / And I did yield to him. But the next morn betimes, / His purpose surfeiting, he sends a warrant / For my poor brother's head.

In short, leaving out the needless detail of how I persuaded him, how I prayed and knelt, how he refused me and how I answered, for this went on a long time, I now begin, with grief and shame, to tell the vile conclusion. He would not release my brother unless I gave my chaste body to his greedy, unrestrained lust. After much struggle my pity for my brother overcame my honour, and I gave in to him. But early the next morning, his desire satisfied, he sent a warrant for my poor brother's head.
O, that it were as like as it is true!
Oh, I wish it were as likely as it is true!

By heaven, fond wretch, thou know'st not what thou speak'st, / Or else thou art suborned against his honour / In hateful practice. First, his integrity / Stands without blemish; next, it imports no reason / That with such vehemency he should pursue / Faults proper to himself. If he had so offended, / He would have weighed thy brother by himself, / And not have cut him off. Someone hath set you on. / Confess the truth, and say by whose advice / Thou cam'st here to complain.

By heaven, foolish wretch, you don't know what you're saying, or else you have been bribed to attack his honour in some hateful plot. First, his integrity is spotless. Second, it makes no sense that he would pursue so fiercely faults that were his own. If he had sinned like that, he would have judged your brother by himself and not had him executed. Someone has put you up to this. Confess the truth, and say on whose advice you came here to complain.

And is this all? / Then, O you blessed ministers above, / Keep me in patience, and with ripened time / Unfold the evil which is here wrapt up / In countenance! Heaven shield your Grace from woe, / As I, thus wronged, hence unbelieved go.

And is this all? Then, oh you blessed angels above, keep me patient, and when the time is ripe reveal the evil that is wrapped up here in favour! Heaven protect your Grace from sorrow, as I, wronged like this, go away unbelieved.

I know you'd fain be gone. An officer! / To prison with her! Shall we thus permit / A blasting and a scandalous breath to fall / On him so near us? This needs must be a practice. / Who knew of your intent and coming hither?
I know you'd like to leave. Officer! Take her to prison! Are we to let a poisonous, scandalous breath fall on a man so close to us? This must be a plot. Who knew you intended to come here?
One that I would were here, Friar Lodowick.
Someone I wish were here: Friar Lodowick.
A ghostly father, belike. Who knows that Lodowick?
A priest, I suppose. Who knows this Lodowick?
My lord, I know him. 'Tis a meddling friar. / I do not like the man. Had he been lay, my lord, / For certain words he spake against your Grace / In your retirement, I had swinged him soundly.

My lord, I know him. He's a meddling friar. I don't like the man. If he hadn't been a churchman, my lord, I would have given him a sound beating for certain things he said against your Grace while you were away.
Words against me? This's a good friar, belike. / And to set on this wretched woman here / Against our substitute! Let this friar be found.
Words against me? He sounds like a fine friar. And setting this wretched woman on to attack our deputy! Find this friar.
But yesternight, my lord, she and that friar, / I saw them at the prison. A saucy friar, / A very scurvy fellow.
Only last night, my lord, I saw her and that friar at the prison. An insolent friar, a really nasty fellow.

Blessed be your royal Grace! / I have stood by, my lord, and I have heard / Your royal ear abused. First hath this woman / Most wrongfully accused your substitute, / Who is as free from touch or soil with her / As she from one ungot.

Blessings on your royal Grace! I have been standing by, my lord, and I have heard your royal ear abused. First, this woman has falsely accused your deputy, who is as innocent of touching or staining her as she is of someone not yet conceived.
We did believe no less. / Know you that Friar Lodowick that she speaks of?
We believed as much. Do you know this Friar Lodowick she talks about?
I know him for a man divine and holy, / Not scurvy, nor a temporary meddler, / As he's reported by this gentleman; / And, on my trust, a man that never yet / Did, as he vouches, misreport your Grace.
I know him as a godly and holy man, not nasty, nor a meddler in worldly affairs, as this gentleman says; and, on my word, a man who has never slandered your Grace, as this man claims.
My lord, most villainously; believe it.
My lord, he slandered you most villainously, believe me.

Well, he in time may come to clear himself; / But at this instant he is sick, my lord, / Of a strange fever. Upon his mere request, / Being come to knowledge that there was complaint / Intended 'gainst Lord Angelo, came I hither / To speak, as from his mouth, what he doth know / Is true and false; and what he with his oath / And all probation will make up full clear / Whensoever he's convented. First, for this woman, / To justify this worthy nobleman, / So vulgarly and personally accused, / Her shall you hear disproved to her eyes, / Till she herself confess it.

Well, he may come in time to clear himself. But just now he is ill, my lord, with a strange fever. At his request alone, having learned that a complaint against Lord Angelo was planned, I came here to say, as if from his own mouth, what he knows to be true and false, and what he will prove with his oath and every kind of evidence whenever he is summoned. First, as for this woman: to clear this worthy nobleman, so publicly and personally accused, you will hear her proved wrong to her face, until she confesses it herself.

Good friar, let's hear it. / Do you not smile at this, Lord Angelo? / O heaven, the vanity of wretched fools! / Give us some seats.—Come, cousin Angelo, / In this I'll be impartial. Be you judge / Of your own cause.

Good friar, let's hear it. Don't you smile at this, Lord Angelo? Oh heaven, the stupidity of wretched fools! Bring us some seats. Come, cousin Angelo, I will take no side in this. You be judge in your own case.
Is this the witness, friar? / First let her show her face, and after speak.
Is this the witness, friar? First let her show her face, and then speak.
Pardon, my lord; I will not show my face / Until my husband bid me.
Forgive me, my lord, I will not show my face until my husband tells me to.
Why, you are nothing then, neither maid, widow, nor wife?
Why, then you are nothing: neither virgin, widow nor wife?
My lord, she may be a punk; for many of them are neither maid, widow, / nor wife.
My lord, she may be a whore, because a lot of them are neither virgin, widow nor wife.
Silence that fellow. I would he had some cause to prattle for himself.
Silence that fellow. I wish he had some reason to babble on his own behalf.
My lord, I do confess I ne'er was married, / And I confess besides, I am no maid. / I have known my husband; yet my husband / Knows not that ever he knew me.
My lord, I admit I have never been married, and I admit too that I am not a virgin. I have slept with my husband, but my husband does not know that he ever slept with me.
He was drunk, then, my lord; it can be no better.
Then he was drunk, my lord; there's no other explanation.
For the benefit of silence, would thou wert so too.
For the sake of some quiet, I wish you were drunk too.
This is no witness for Lord Angelo.
This is no witness for Lord Angelo.

Now I come to't, my lord. / She that accuses him of fornication / In self-same manner doth accuse my husband, / And charges him, my lord, with such a time / When I'll depose I had him in mine arms / With all th' effect of love.

I am coming to that, my lord. The woman who accuses him of fornication is accusing my husband in exactly the same way, and she names a time, my lord, when I will swear I had him in my arms, with all the acts of love.
Is she accusing anyone else besides me?
Why, just, my lord, and that is Angelo, / Who thinks he knows that he ne'er knew my body, / But knows, he thinks, that he knows Isabel's.
Yes, exactly, my lord, and that is Angelo, who thinks he knows he never slept with me, but thinks he knows he slept with Isabel.
This is a strange abuse. Let's see thy face.
This is a strange slander. Let's see your face.

My husband bids me; now I will unmask. [Unveiling] / This is that face, thou cruel Angelo, / Which once thou swor'st was worth the looking on. / This is the hand which, with a vowed contract, / Was fast belocked in thine. This is the body / That took away the match from Isabel / And did supply thee at thy garden-house / In her imagined person.

My husband tells me to; now I will unmask. (She takes off her veil) This is the face, cruel Angelo, that you once swore was worth looking at. This is the hand that was locked tight in yours by a sworn contract. This is the body that took Isabel's place in the meeting and satisfied you in your garden house, while you imagined it was her.

My lord, I must confess I know this woman; / And five years since there was some speech of marriage / Betwixt myself and her; which was broke off, / Partly for that her promised proportions / Came short of composition; but in chief / For that her reputation was disvalued / In levity. Since which time of five years / I never spake with her, saw her, nor heard from her, / Upon my faith and honour.

My lord, I must admit I know this woman. Five years ago there was some talk of marriage between her and me. It was broken off, partly because her promised dowry fell short of what had been agreed, but mainly because her reputation was damaged by reports of loose behaviour. Since then, in five years, I have never spoken to her, seen her or heard from her, on my faith and honour.

Noble Prince, / As there comes light from heaven and words from breath, / As there is sense in truth and truth in virtue, / I am affianced this man's wife as strongly / As words could make up vows. And, my good lord, / But Tuesday night last gone, in's garden-house, / He knew me as a wife. As this is true, / Let me in safety raise me from my knees, / Or else for ever be confixed here, / A marble monument!

Noble prince, as surely as light comes from heaven and words from breath, as surely as there is meaning in truth and truth in virtue, I am this man's promised wife, as firmly as words could make vows. And, my good lord, only last Tuesday night, in his garden house, he slept with me as his wife. If this is true, let me rise safely from my knees; if not, let me be fixed here for ever, a marble statue!

I did but smile till now. / Now, good my lord, give me the scope of justice. / My patience here is touched. I do perceive / These poor informal women are no more / But instruments of some more mightier member / That sets them on. Let me have way, my lord, / To find this practice out.

Up to now I have only smiled. Now, my good lord, give me full power to do justice. My patience is wearing thin. I can see that these poor, foolish women are only the tools of some more powerful person who has put them up to this. Give me leave, my lord, to uncover this plot.

Ay, with my heart; / And punish them to your height of pleasure. / Thou foolish friar, and thou pernicious woman, / Compact with her that's gone, think'st thou thy oaths, / Though they would swear down each particular saint, / Were testimonies against his worth and credit, / That's sealed in approbation? You, Lord Escalus, / Sit with my cousin; lend him your kind pains / To find out this abuse, whence 'tis derived. / There is another friar that set them on; / Let him be sent for.

Yes, with all my heart; and punish them as much as you like. You foolish friar, and you wicked woman, in league with the one who has gone: do you think your oaths, even if they swore by every single saint, could count as evidence against his worth and good name, which have been sealed by long approval? You, Lord Escalus, sit with my cousin and lend him your kind help to find out where this slander comes from. There is another friar who put them up to it; send for him.
Would he were here, my lord; for he indeed / Hath set the women on to this complaint. / Your Provost knows the place where he abides, / And he may fetch him.
I wish he were here, my lord, because he really did set the women on to make this complaint. Your Provost knows where he lives and can fetch him.

And you, my noble and well-warranted cousin, / Whom it concerns to hear this matter forth, / Do with your injuries as seems you best / In any chastisement. I for a while / Will leave you; but stir not you till you have / Well determined upon these slanderers.

And you, my noble cousin, whose good name is well proven and who has every right to hear this matter through, punish these injuries to you however you think best. I will leave you for a while; but don't move until you have dealt thoroughly with these slanderers.
My lord, we'll do it throughly.
My lord, we'll do it thoroughly.
Signior Lucio, did not you say you knew that Friar Lodowick to be a / dishonest person?
Signior Lucio, didn't you say you knew this Friar Lodowick to be a dishonest man?
Cucullus non facit monachum, honest in nothing but in his clothes, / and one that hath spoke most villainous speeches of the Duke.
The hood doesn't make the monk. He's honest in nothing but his clothes, and he has said the most villainous things about the Duke.
We shall entreat you to abide here till he come, and enforce them / against him. We shall find this friar a notable fellow.
We will ask you to stay here until he comes, and repeat those charges against him. We'll find this friar is a notorious fellow.
As any in Vienna, on my word.
As notorious as any in Vienna, on my word.
Call that same Isabel here once again. I would speak with her.
Call that Isabel here again. I want to speak to her.
Pray you, my lord, give me leave to question; you shall see how I'll / handle her.
Please, my lord, let me question her. You'll see how I handle her.
Not better than he, by her own report.
Not better than he did, by her own account.
Marry, sir, I think, if you handled her privately, she would sooner / confess; perchance, publicly, she'll be ashamed.
Why, sir, I think if you handled her in private, she'd confess sooner. In public, perhaps, she'll be ashamed.
I will go darkly to work with her.
I will work on her subtly.
That's the way; for women are light at midnight.
That's the way, because women are light (and loose) at midnight.
[To Isabella] Come on, mistress, here's a gentlewoman denies all / that you have said.
(To Isabella) Come on, mistress, here's a lady who denies everything you said.
My lord, here comes the rascal I spoke of, here with the Provost.
My lord, here comes the rascal I told you about, with the Provost.
In very good time. Speak not you to him till we call upon you.
At just the right time. Don't speak to him until we call on you.
Come, sir, did you set these women on to slander Lord Angelo? They have / confessed you did.
Come, sir, did you put these women up to slandering Lord Angelo? They have confessed that you did.
How! Know you where you are?
What! Do you know where you are?
Respect to your great place; and let the devil / Be sometime honoured for his burning throne. / Where is the Duke? 'Tis he should hear me speak.
I respect your high position; and the devil too is sometimes honoured for his burning throne. Where is the Duke? He is the one who should hear me.
The Duke's in us; and we will hear you speak. / Look you speak justly.
The Duke's power is in us, and we will hear you. Make sure you speak fairly.

Boldly, at least. But, O, poor souls, / Come you to seek the lamb here of the fox, / Good night to your redress! Is the Duke gone? / Then is your cause gone too. The Duke's unjust / Thus to retort your manifest appeal, / And put your trial in the villain's mouth / Which here you come to accuse.

Boldly, at least. But oh, poor souls, have you come to ask the fox for the lamb? Then say goodbye to any remedy! Has the Duke gone? Then your case has gone too. The Duke is unjust to throw back your open appeal like this and leave your trial in the mouth of the villain you came here to accuse.
This is the rascal; this is he I spoke of.
This is the rascal; this is the one I told you about.

Why, thou unreverend and unhallowed friar, / Is't not enough thou hast suborned these women / To accuse this worthy man, but, in foul mouth, / And in the witness of his proper ear, / To call him villain? And then to glance from him / To th' Duke himself, to tax him with injustice? / Take him hence! To th' rack with him! We'll touse you / Joint by joint, but we will know his purpose. / What! Unjust?

Why, you irreverent, unholy friar! Isn't it enough that you bribed these women to accuse this worthy man, but you must call him a villain with your foul mouth, in his own hearing? And then turn from him to the Duke himself and accuse him of injustice? Take him away! To the rack with him! We'll pull you apart joint by joint, but we'll find out what he's up to. What! Unjust?

Be not so hot. The Duke / Dare no more stretch this finger of mine than he / Dare rack his own. His subject am I not, / Nor here provincial. My business in this state / Made me a looker-on here in Vienna, / Where I have seen corruption boil and bubble / Till it o'errun the stew. Laws for all faults, / But faults so countenanced that the strong statutes / Stand like the forfeits in a barber's shop, / As much in mock as mark.

Don't be so hot. The Duke would no more dare to stretch this finger of mine than he would dare to rack his own. I am not his subject, nor under the authority of this province. My business in this state made me an observer here in Vienna, where I have seen corruption boil and bubble until it overflows the pot. There are laws for every fault, but faults are so tolerated that the strong statutes are like the list of penalties hanging in a barber's shop, as much laughed at as noticed.
Slander to the state! Away with him to prison!
Slander against the state! Take him away to prison!
What can you vouch against him, Signior Lucio? / Is this the man that you did tell us of?
What can you say against him, Signior Lucio? Is this the man you told us about?
'Tis he, my lord. Come hither, goodman Baldpate. / Do you know me?
That's him, my lord. Come here, Mister Baldhead. Do you know me?
I remember you, sir, by the sound of your voice. I met you at the / prison, in the absence of the Duke.
I remember you, sir, by the sound of your voice. I met you at the prison while the Duke was away.
O did you so? And do you remember what you said of the Duke?
Oh, did you? And do you remember what you said about the Duke?
Do you so, sir? And was the Duke a fleshmonger, a fool, and a coward, / as you then reported him to be?
Do you, sir? And was the Duke a lecher, a fool and a coward, as you said then?
You must, sir, change persons with me ere you make that my report. You / indeed spoke so of him, and much more, much worse.
You must change places with me, sir, before you can call that my report. It was you who said that about him, and much more, much worse.
O thou damnable fellow! Did not I pluck thee by the nose for thy / speeches?
Oh, you damnable fellow! Didn't I pull your nose for what you said?
I protest I love the Duke as I love myself.
I swear I love the Duke as I love myself.
Hark how the villain would close now, after his treasonable abuses!
Listen to how the villain tries to make peace now, after his treasonous insults!

Such a fellow is not to be talked withal. Away with him to prison! / Where is the provost? Away with him to prison! Lay bolts enough upon / him. Let him speak no more. Away with those giglets too, and with the / other confederate companion!

There's no talking with a fellow like this. Take him away to prison! Where is the Provost? Take him away to prison! Put plenty of chains on him. Don't let him speak any more. Take those flirts away too, and the other accomplice!
What, resists he? Help him, Lucio.
What, is he resisting? Help him, Lucio.

Come, sir, come, sir, come, sir. Foh, sir! Why, you bald-pated lying / rascal! You must be hooded, must you? Show your knave's visage, with a / pox to you! Show your sheep-biting face, and be hanged an hour! Will't / not off?

Come on, sir, come on, sir, come on, sir. Ugh, sir! Why, you bald-headed lying rascal! You have to wear a hood, do you? Show your villain's face, damn you! Show your sheep-killing face, and be hanged in an hour! Won't it come off?
Thou art the first knave that e'er mad'st a duke. / First, Provost, let me bail these gentle three. / [To Lucio] Sneak not away, sir, for the friar and you / Must have a word anon.—Lay hold on him.
You are the first villain who ever made a duke. First, Provost, let me release these three good people. (To Lucio) Don't sneak away, sir; the friar and you must have a word shortly. Hold him.
This may prove worse than hanging.
This may turn out worse than hanging.

[To Escalus] What you have spoke I pardon. Sit you down. / We'll borrow place of him. [To Angelo] Sir, by your leave. / Hast thou or word, or wit, or impudence, / That yet can do thee office? If thou hast, / Rely upon it till my tale be heard, / And hold no longer out.

(To Escalus) I pardon what you said. Sit down. We'll borrow his seat. (To Angelo) Sir, if you'll allow me. Have you any word, wit or nerve left that can still serve you? If you have, rely on it until my story has been heard, and then hold out no longer.

O my dread lord, / I should be guiltier than my guiltiness / To think I can be undiscernible, / When I perceive your Grace, like power divine, / Hath looked upon my passes. Then, good Prince, / No longer session hold upon my shame, / But let my trial be mine own confession. / Immediate sentence then, and sequent death / Is all the grace I beg.

Oh, my dread lord, I would be guiltier than my guilt if I thought I could stay hidden, now that I see your Grace, like God, has watched all my actions. So, good prince, do not keep my shame on trial any longer, but let my own confession be my trial. An immediate sentence and death to follow are all the mercy I ask for.
Come hither, Mariana. / Say, wast thou e'er contracted to this woman?
Come here, Mariana. Tell me, were you ever contracted to this woman?
Go, take her hence and marry her instantly. / Do you the office, friar; which consummate, / Return him here again.—Go with him, Provost.
Go, take her away and marry her at once. Friar, you perform the ceremony; and when it is done, bring him back here. Go with him, Provost.
My lord, I am more amazed at his dishonour / Than at the strangeness of it.
My lord, I am more amazed at his dishonour than at the strangeness of all this.
Come hither, Isabel. / Your friar is now your prince. As I was then / Advertising and holy to your business, / Not changing heart with habit, I am still / Attorneyed at your service.

Come here, Isabel. Your friar is now your prince. Just as I was then devoted to your business, both as adviser and as holy man, I have not changed my heart along with my clothes, and I am still at your service as your advocate.
O, give me pardon, / That I, your vassal, have employed and pained / Your unknown sovereignty.
Oh, forgive me that I, your subject, have used and troubled you without knowing you were my sovereign.

You are pardoned, Isabel. / And now, dear maid, be you as free to us. / Your brother's death, I know, sits at your heart, / And you may marvel why I obscured myself, / Labouring to save his life, and would not rather / Make rash remonstrance of my hidden power / Than let him so be lost. O most kind maid, / It was the swift celerity of his death, / Which I did think with slower foot came on, / That brained my purpose. But peace be with him. / That life is better life, past fearing death, / Than that which lives to fear. Make it your comfort, / So happy is your brother.

You are forgiven, Isabel. And now, dear maiden, forgive me as freely. I know your brother's death weighs on your heart, and you may wonder why I kept myself hidden while working to save his life, rather than suddenly revealing my secret power and not letting him be lost like that. Oh, kindest of maidens, it was the sudden speed of his death, which I thought was coming more slowly, that dashed out my plan. But peace be with him. A life beyond the fear of death is a better life than one that lives in fear. Take comfort from that: your brother is happy.

For this new-married man approaching here, / Whose salt imagination yet hath wronged / Your well-defended honour, you must pardon / For Mariana's sake. But as he adjudged your brother, / Being criminal in double violation / Of sacred chastity and of promise-breach / Thereon dependent, for your brother's life, / The very mercy of the law cries out / Most audible, even from his proper tongue, / "An Angelo for Claudio, death for death." / Haste still pays haste, and leisure answers leisure; / Like doth quit like, and measure still for measure. / Then, Angelo, thy fault's thus manifested, / Which, though thou wouldst deny, denies thee vantage. / We do condemn thee to the very block / Where Claudio stooped to death, and with like haste. / Away with him.

As for this newly married man coming here, whose lustful imagination wronged your well-defended honour, you must forgive him for Mariana's sake. But because he condemned your brother, while he himself was guilty twice over, of violating sacred chastity and of breaking the promise that depended on it, to spare your brother's life, the very mercy of the law cries out loud and clear, even in his own words: "An Angelo for Claudio, death for death." Haste always pays for haste, and delay answers delay; like repays like, and always measure for measure. So, Angelo, your crime is plain, and even if you denied it, the denial would do you no good. We condemn you to the very block where Claudio bowed to death, and with the same haste. Take him away.
O my most gracious lord, / I hope you will not mock me with a husband.
Oh, my most gracious lord, I hope you are not mocking me by giving me a husband.

It is your husband mocked you with a husband. / Consenting to the safeguard of your honour, / I thought your marriage fit. Else imputation, / For that he knew you, might reproach your life, / And choke your good to come. For his possessions, / Although by confiscation they are ours, / We do instate and widow you with all / To buy you a better husband.

It was your husband who mocked you with a husband. To protect your honour, I thought this marriage right. Otherwise, because he slept with you, gossip might shame you for life and choke the good fortune still to come for you. As for his property, though it is ours by confiscation, we give it all to you as his widow, to buy you a better husband.
O my dear lord, / I crave no other, nor no better man.
Oh, my dear lord, I want no other and no better man.
Never crave him; we are definitive.
Don't ask for him; our decision is final.
You do but lose your labour. / Away with him to death. [To Lucio] Now, sir, to you.
You are only wasting your effort. Take him away to his death. (To Lucio) Now, sir, it's your turn.
O my good lord.—Sweet Isabel, take my part; / Lend me your knees, and all my life to come / I'll lend you all my life to do you service.
Oh, my good lord! Sweet Isabel, take my side. Lend me your knees, and all my life to come I'll give my whole life to serving you.
Against all sense you do importune her. / Should she kneel down in mercy of this fact, / Her brother's ghost his paved bed would break, / And take her hence in horror.
You are begging her against all reason. If she knelt to ask mercy for this deed, her brother's ghost would break out of his stone grave and carry her off in horror.

Isabel, / Sweet Isabel, do yet but kneel by me; / Hold up your hands, say nothing. I'll speak all. / They say best men are moulded out of faults, / And, for the most, become much more the better / For being a little bad. So may my husband. / O Isabel, will you not lend a knee?

Isabel, sweet Isabel, only kneel beside me. Hold up your hands and say nothing; I'll do all the speaking. They say the best men are made out of faults, and most of them become much better for being a little bad. So may my husband. Oh, Isabel, won't you lend me a knee?

[Kneeling] Most bounteous sir, / Look, if it please you, on this man condemned / As if my brother lived. I partly think / A due sincerity governed his deeds / Till he did look on me. Since it is so, / Let him not die. My brother had but justice, / In that he did the thing for which he died. / For Angelo, / His act did not o'ertake his bad intent, / And must be buried but as an intent / That perished by the way. Thoughts are no subjects; / Intents but merely thoughts.

(Kneeling) Most generous sir, if you please, look on this condemned man as if my brother were alive. I partly think a real sincerity ruled his actions until he looked at me. Since that is so, don't let him die. My brother received only justice, because he did the thing he died for. As for Angelo, his act did not carry out his evil intention, and must be buried as an intention that died on the way. Thoughts are not subject to the law, and intentions are only thoughts.
Your suit's unprofitable. Stand up, I say. / I have bethought me of another fault. / Provost, how came it Claudio was beheaded / At an unusual hour?
Your plea does no good. Stand up, I tell you. I have thought of another crime. Provost, how did it happen that Claudio was beheaded at an unusual hour?
Had you a special warrant for the deed?
Did you have a special warrant for it?
No, my good lord, it was by private message.
No, my good lord, it came by private message.
For which I do discharge you of your office. / Give up your keys.
For that I dismiss you from your post. Hand over your keys.

Pardon me, noble lord. / I thought it was a fault, but knew it not; / Yet did repent me after more advice. / For testimony whereof, one in the prison / That should by private order else have died, / I have reserved alive.

Forgive me, noble lord. I thought it was wrong, but I wasn't sure; and on further thought I regretted it. As proof of that, I have kept alive one man in the prison who would otherwise have died by private order.
I would thou hadst done so by Claudio. / Go fetch him hither, let me look upon him.
I wish you had done the same for Claudio. Go and fetch him here; let me see him.
I am sorry one so learned and so wise / As you, Lord Angelo, have still appeared, / Should slip so grossly, both in the heat of blood / And lack of tempered judgement afterward.
I am sorry, Lord Angelo, that a man as learned and wise as you have always seemed should slip so badly, both in the heat of passion and in your lack of balanced judgment afterwards.
I am sorry that such sorrow I procure, / And so deep sticks it in my penitent heart / That I crave death more willingly than mercy; / 'Tis my deserving, and I do entreat it.
I am sorry to cause such sorrow, and it sticks so deep in my repentant heart that I ask for death more willingly than mercy. It is what I deserve, and I beg for it.

There was a friar told me of this man. / Sirrah, thou art said to have a stubborn soul / That apprehends no further than this world, / And squar'st thy life according. Thou'rt condemned; / But, for those earthly faults, I quit them all, / And pray thee take this mercy to provide / For better times to come. Friar, advise him; / I leave him to your hand.—What muffled fellow's that?

A friar told me about this man. Fellow, they say you have a stubborn soul that sees nothing beyond this world, and that you shape your life to match. You are condemned; but I pardon all those earthly crimes, and ask you to use this mercy to prepare for better times to come. Friar, advise him; I leave him in your hands. Who is that muffled fellow?
This is another prisoner that I saved, / Who should have died when Claudio lost his head; / As like almost to Claudio as himself.
This is another prisoner I saved, who should have died when Claudio lost his head. He is almost as like Claudio as Claudio himself.

[To Isabella] If he be like your brother, for his sake / Is he pardoned; and for your lovely sake, / Give me your hand and say you will be mine. / He is my brother too. But fitter time for that. / By this Lord Angelo perceives he's safe; / Methinks I see a quick'ning in his eye. / Well, Angelo, your evil quits you well. / Look that you love your wife, her worth worth yours. / I find an apt remission in myself. / And yet here's one in place I cannot pardon. / [To Lucio] You, sirrah, that knew me for a fool, a coward, / One all of luxury, an ass, a madman. / Wherein have I so deserved of you / That you extol me thus?

(To Isabella) If he is like your brother, he is pardoned for your brother's sake; and for your lovely sake, give me your hand and say you will be mine, and he will be my brother too. But there will be a better time for that. By now Lord Angelo realises he is safe; I think I see life coming back into his eyes. Well, Angelo, your sin has paid you back well. Make sure you love your wife; her worth equals yours. I find myself ready to forgive. And yet there is one here I cannot pardon. (To Lucio) You, fellow, who knew me for a fool, a coward, a man full of lust, an ass, a madman: what have I done to you that you should praise me like this?
Faith, my lord, I spoke it but according to the trick. If you will hang / me for it, you may, but I had rather it would please you I might be / whipped.
Honestly, my lord, I only said it as a joke, as is the fashion. If you want to hang me for it, you can, but I'd rather you were pleased to have me whipped.

Whipped first, sir, and hanged after. / Proclaim it, Provost, round about the city, / If any woman wronged by this lewd fellow, / As I have heard him swear himself there's one / Whom he begot with child—let her appear, / And he shall marry her. The nuptial finished, / Let him be whipped and hanged.

Whipped first, sir, and hanged after. Provost, have it announced throughout the city that if any woman has been wronged by this lewd fellow (I have heard him swear himself that there is one he got pregnant), she should come forward, and he shall marry her. When the wedding is over, let him be whipped and hanged.
I beseech your Highness, do not marry me to a whore. Your highness said / even now I made you a duke; good my lord, do not recompense me in / making me a cuckold.
I beg your Highness, don't marry me to a whore. Your Highness said just now that I made you a duke. My good lord, don't pay me back by making me a cuckold.
Upon mine honour, thou shalt marry her. / Thy slanders I forgive, and therewithal / Remit thy other forfeits.—Take him to prison, / And see our pleasure herein executed.
On my honour, you shall marry her. I forgive your slanders, and with them I let off your other penalties. Take him to prison and see that our wishes are carried out.
Marrying a punk, my lord, is pressing to death, whipping, and hanging.
Marrying a whore, my lord, is like being pressed to death, whipped and hanged all at once.

She, Claudio, that you wronged, look you restore. / Joy to you, Mariana! Love her, Angelo. / I have confessed her, and I know her virtue. / Thanks, good friend Escalus, for thy much goodness; / There's more behind that is more gratulate. / Thanks, Provost, for thy care and secrecy; / We shall employ thee in a worthier place. / Forgive him, Angelo, that brought you home / The head of Ragozine for Claudio's. / Th' offence pardons itself. Dear Isabel, / I have a motion much imports your good; / Whereto if you'll a willing ear incline, / What's mine is yours, and what is yours is mine. / So, bring us to our palace, where we'll show / What's yet behind that's meet you all should know.

Claudio, make sure you make amends to the woman you wronged. Joy to you, Mariana! Love her, Angelo. I have heard her confession, and I know how good she is. Thank you, my good friend Escalus, for all your goodness; there is more reward to come, more worth celebrating. Thank you, Provost, for your care and your secrecy; we will give you a worthier post. Forgive him, Angelo, for bringing you the head of Ragozine instead of Claudio's. The offence pardons itself. Dear Isabel, I have a proposal that greatly concerns your good. If you will lend it a willing ear, what is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine. So, take us to our palace, where we will reveal what still remains that you should all know.
